content: Here is a file with another file hidden inside it. Can you extract it? TL;DR Binwalk is an introductory digital forensics challenge that focuses on file carving and detecting embedded artifacts within image containers. Inspecting the file headers reveals an anomaly where a PNG file is masquerading under a .jpeg extension with extra data trailing the IEND chunk. Carving the hidden binary via foremost or binwalk extracts a secondary image displaying the flag.
title: Binwalk

content: File Analysis We are given an image file named PurpleThing.jpeg . We begin by examining the file’s metadata and structure using exiftool : exiftool PurpleThing.jpeg ExifTool Version Number : 13.25 File Name : PurpleThing.jpeg File Size : 165 kB File Type : PNG File Type Extension : png MIME Type : image/png Image Width : 780 Image Height : 720 Warning : [minor] Trailer data after PNG IEND chunk Two critical anomalies stand out: Mismatched File Extension: Despite having a .jpeg extension, the magic bytes identify the container as a PNG image. Trailer Data Warning: ExifTool reports [minor] Trailer data after PNG IEND chunk . In the PNG file specification, the IEND chunk marks the valid end of the image stream. Any bytes appended after IEND represent appended or concatenated data—frequently indicating an embedded file payload.
title: Binwalk

content: Carving the Embedded Data We can carve embedded files out of the container using file carving tools such as foremost or binwalk : foremost PurpleThing.jpeg foremost automatically scans for known headers and footers, extracting two distinct PNG files into output/png/ : 00000000.png 00000299.png 00000000.png represents the original outer image. 00000299.png is the hidden payload embedded at offset 299 . content: A peculiar file filled with punctuation marks holds the key. Can you decipher this multi-layered esoteric program? TL;DR Brain Dead is an esoteric programming language challenge. The source file brain_dead.bf is composed of 2-character compressed Ook! symbol pairs ( .? , !! , ?! ). Decoding these pairs into Brainfuck and executing them in a Python virtual tape interpreter produces an intermediate script written with custom language tokens. Interpreting this second stage yields decimal ASCII codes, which assemble into the final flag.
title: Brain Dead

content: 1. Challenge File Inspection The challenge file brain_dead.bf contains sequences composed exclusively of three punctuation characters: . , ? , and ! : .?... ..... ..!.? ..... ..!?! ... This character set corresponds directly to Ook!, a Brainfuck dialect that uses pairs of punctuation marks.
title: Brain Dead

content: 2. Deciphering the Grammar Standard OK! uses words such as Ook. Ook? . In this challenge, the words have been compressed into raw punctuation pairs: OK! Pair Brainfuck Instructions Functions .? > Increment memory pointer ?. < Decrement memory pointer .. + Increment bytes at pointer !! - Decrement byte at pointer !. . Output bytes at pointer .! , Read bytes into pointer !? [ Jump forward if pointer byte is zero ?! ] Jump backward if pointer byte is non-zero
title: Brain Dead

content: 3. The Multi-Stage Execution Pipeline Running the converted Brainfuck code does not immediately reveal plaintext. Instead, the first execution stage emits an intermediate script containing repetitive string tokens: stage1 output: token-based script These intermediate tokens map back to Brainfuck operations, which in turn generate a series of decimal numbers. Converting those decimal values ​​to their corresponding ASCII characters uncovers the flag.
title: Brain Dead

content: 4. Complete Automated Solver We construct a multi-stage Python emulator: #!/usr/bin/env python3 import re OOK_MAP = { (".", "?"): ">", ("?", "."): "<", (".", "."): "+", ("!", "!"): "-", ("!", "."): ".", (".", "!"): ",", ("!", "?"): "[", ("?", "!"): "]", } TOKEN_MAP = { "zero": ">", "one": "<", "two": "+", "three": "-", "four": ".", "five": ",", "six": "[", "seven": "]", } def run_brainfuck(code): tape = [0] * 30000 ptr = 0 pc = 0 output = [] brackets = {} stack = [] for i, c in enumerate(code): if c == "[": stack.append(i) elif c == "]": start = stack.pop() brackets[start] = i brackets[i] = start while pc < len(code): cmd = code[pc] if cmd == ">": ptr += 1 elif cmd == "<": ptr -= 1 elif cmd == "+": tape[ptr] = (tape[ptr] + 1) & 0xFF elif cmd == "-": tape[ptr] = (tape[ptr] - 1) & 0xFF elif cmd == ".": output.append(chr(tape[ptr])) elif cmd == "[" and tape[ptr] == 0: pc = brackets[pc] elif cmd == "]" and tape[ptr] != 0: pc = brackets[pc] pc += 1 return "".join(output) def ook_to_bf(data): clean = [c for c in data if c in ".?!"] return "".join( OOK_MAP[(clean[i], clean[i + 1])] for i in range(0, len(clean), 2) ) def tokens_to_bf(s): s = s.lower() i = 0 out = [] tokens = sorted(TOKEN_MAP.keys(), key=len, reverse=True) while i < len(s): for t in tokens: if s.startswith(t, i): out.append(TOKEN_MAP[t]) i += len(t) break else: i += 1 return "".join(out) def nums_to_ascii(s): nums = list(map(int, re.findall(r"\d+", s))) return "".join(map(chr, nums)) if __name__ == "__main__": raw_data = open("brain_dead.bf", "r", encoding="utf-8").read() # Stage 1: Compressed Ook! -> Brainfuck -> execute stage1 = run_brainfuck(ook_to_bf(raw_data)) # Stage 2: Tokens -> Brainfuck -> execute stage2 = run_brainfuck(tokens_to_bf(stage1)) # Stage 3: Numeric ASCII code conversion flag = nums_to_ascii(stage2) print("[+] Flag:", flag) Running the script: python3 decode.py Output: [+] Flag: FGTE{BRAIN_GO_BRRR}
title: Brain Dead

content: Flag FGTE{BRAIN_GO_BRRR}
title: Brain Dead

content: TL;DR Flip-Flop is a crypto challenge from FGTE. Challenge provides files:
title: Flip-Flop

content: Challenge Description Challenge provides files: cipher.txt (contains ciphertext in bytes / non-printable characters) chall.py (encryption script) From chall.py , it is known that ciphertext is created by processing each plaintext character into 8-bit binary, then reversing the bit order (bit-reversal).
title: Flip-Flop

content: Solution Steps
title: Flip-Flop

content: 1. Encryption Algorithm Analysis The main contents of the encode() function: bits = f"{ord(c):08b}" # ubah char ke biner 8-bit rev = bits[::-1] # balik urutan bit out.append(chr(int(rev, 2))) Meaning: each character → 8-bit binary bits reversed (example 01000001 → 10000010 ) the result is converted back to bytes/char Because the bit-reversal operation is involutive (flipped twice back to its initial form), the decode function is exactly the same as the encode.
title: Flip-Flop

content: 2. Create a Decryption Script To return plaintext: Read cipher.txt in binary mode Decode using latin-1 so that bytes 0–255 are not damaged Run the same bit-reversal process Scripts: def decode(text: str) -> str: out = [] for c in text: bits = f"{ord(c):08b}" rev = bits[::-1] out.append(chr(int(rev, 2))) return "".join(out) if __name__ == "__main__": with open("cipher.txt", "rb") as f: cipher = f.read().decode("latin-1") plain = decode(cipher) print(plain)
title: Flip-Flop

content: Extract the flag from the Gandalf.jpg file. You may need to write a quick script to solve this. TL;DR GandalfTheWise is an intermediate steganography challenge that embeds multiple JPEG comment markers ( 0xFFFE ) containing Base64-encoded strings. Decoding the first comment reveals a decoy flag and hint: ___FL0X___ . Decoding the second and third comments into raw byte buffers and computing their byte-by-byte XOR reveals the true flag.
title: GandalfTheWise

content: 1. Visual & Metadata Inspection The provided image Gandalf.jpg displays an image of Gandalf. Opening the file in standard photo viewers reveals no obvious visual artifacts or watermarks.
title: GandalfTheWise

content: 2. File Structure & Header Analysis We examine the file’s raw byte stream using xxd : xxd Gandalf.jpg | head -n 12 00000000: ffd8 ffe0 0010 4a46 4946 0001 0100 0001 ......JFIF...... 00000010: 0001 0000 fffe 002b 5131 5247 6247 5668 .......+Q1RGbGVh 00000020: 636d 3537 6547 3979 5832 6c7a 5833 6c76 cm57eG9yX2lzX3lv 00000030: 6458 4a66 5a6e 4a70 5a57 356b 6651 6f3d dXJfZnJpZW5kfQo= 00000040: 0aff fe00 2b78 4436 6b66 4f32 5572 4535 ....+xD6kfO2UrE5 00000050: 536e 4c51 3657 6745 534b 346b 7644 2f59 SnLQ6WgESK4kvD/Y 00000060: 2f72 444a 5058 4e55 3435 6b2f 700a fffe /rDJPXNU45k/p... 00000070: 002b 6832 7269 4549 6a31 3369 4170 3239 .+h2riEIj13iAp29 00000080: 5655 506d 422b 5461 6474 5a70 7064 7733 VUPmB+TadtZppdw3 In the JPEG specification, the marker sequence FF FE defines a Comment Section (COM) containing arbitrary metadata. We observe three distinct comment sections containing Base64-encoded text: 1: Q1RGbGVhcm57eG9yX2lzX3lvdXJfZnJpZW5kfQo= 2: xD6kfO2UrE5SnLQ6WgESK4kvD/Y/rDJPXNU45k/p 3: h2riEIj13iAp29VUPmB+TadtZppdw3AuO7JRiDyU
title: GandalfTheWise

content: 3. Decoding the First Comment (The Hint) Decoding comment 1: echo "Q1RGbGVhcm57eG9yX2lzX3lvdXJfZnJpZW5kfQo=" | base64 -d Output: CTFlearn{xor_is_your_friend} Submitting this value on CTFlearn fails. The text serves as an explicit clue informing us that the remaining two comments must be combined using the XOR operation.
title: GandalfTheWise

content: 4. Byte-wise XORing Comments 2 and 3 We decode comments 2 and 3 to their raw hexadecimal representations: echo "xD6kfO2UrE5SnLQ6WgESK4kvD/Y/rDJPXNU45k/p" | base64 -d | xxd -p c43ea47ced94ac4e529cb43a5a01122b892f0ff63fac324f5cd538e64fe9 echo "h2riEIj13iAp29VUPmB+TadtZppdw3AuO7JRiDyU" | base64 -d | xxd -p 876ae21088f5de2029dbd5543e607e4da76d669a5dc3702e3bb251883c94 We compute the bitwise XOR between these two equal-length hex strings: Using Python to perform the XOR: s1 = bytes.fromhex( "c43ea47ced94ac4e529cb43a5a01122b892f0ff63fac324f5cd538e64fe9" ) s2 = bytes.fromhex( "876ae21088f5de2029dbd5543e607e4da76d669a5dc3702e3bb251883c94" ) result = bytes([a ^ b for a, b in zip(s1, s2)]) print(result.decode()) Output: CTFlearn{Gandalf.BilboBaggins} ##Flags CTFlearn{Gandalf.BilboBaggins}

content: The flag used to be there. But then I redacted it. Good Luck. TL;DR Git Is Good is a version control forensics challenge. After extracting the provided archive, we discover a .git repository folder. While the working tree file flag.txt only contains a decoy ___FL0X___ , inspecting the commit history using git log and diffing previous revisions with git show reveals the original plaintext flag before it was overwritten.
title: Git Is Good

content: Initial Analysis We are given a ZIP archive named gitIsGood.zip . Extracting the archive produces the following directory structure: gitIsGood/ ├── .git/ └── flag.txt Reading the contents of flag.txt : cat flag.txt Output: flag{REDACTED} The file contains only a redacted placeholder. However, the presence of the .git/ folder indicates that the full repository history and metadata have been preserved.
title: Git Is Good

content: Investigating Git Commit History In Git, modifying or deleting a file in a new commit does not remove the data from the repository’s history unless the object database is purged with a history rewrite (such as git filter-repo ). We review the commit history with git log : git log --oneline Output: d10f77c (HEAD -> master) Edited files 195dd65 Edited files 6e824db edited files Three successive commits modified the project files.
title: Git Is Good

content: Analyzing Commit Diffs To see what changes occurred in the most recent commit ( d10f77c ), we inspect its patch diff using git show : git show d10f77c4e766705ab36c7f31dc47b0c5056666bb Output: commit d10f77c4e766705ab36c7f31dc47b0c5056666bb (HEAD -> master) Author: LaScalaLuke <lascala.luke@gmail.com> Date: Sun Oct 30 14:33:18 2016 -0400 Edited files diff --git a/flag.txt b/flag.txt index 8684e68..c5250d0 100644 --- a/flag.txt +++ b/flag.txt @@ -1 +1 @@ -flag{protect_your_git} +flag{REDACTED} The diff clearly shows the removed line prefixed with - : -flag{protect_your_git} The flag was simply modified in the latest commit, leaving the original secret completely preserved in Git’s historical tree objects. ##Flags flag{protect_your_git}
title: Git Is Good

content: Key Takeaways Git Retains Full History: Removing a password, API token, or secret in a subsequent commit does not secure it. Anyone with access to the repository clone can checkout or diff previous commits. Proper Secret Revocation & Purging: When a credential is accidentally committed to version control: Immediately revoke and rotate the secret. Use specialized tools like git-filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner to permanently scrub objects from the Git database if repository scrubbing is required. Add sensitive file patterns to .gitignore to prevent inadvertent tracking.
title: Git Is Good

content: TL;DR Red Channel is a misc challenge from FGTE. —
title: Red Channel

content: Challenge Description The Challenge provides a ZIP file containing multiple sequential PNG images ( img_000.png to img_055.png ). The title of the challenge refers to steganography techniques using red channel.
title: Red Channel

content: Files RedChannel.zip - img_000.png … img_055.png —
title: Red Channel

content: Solution Steps
title: Red Channel

content: 1. Extract ZIP First, extract the archive To view all available files. unzip RedChannel.zip ls The result is dozens of PNG files with the naming pattern img_XXX.png .
title: Red Channel

content: 2. Initial Analysis of File Patterns The number of images arranged sequentially usually indicates: each image stores a portion of the message (e.g. 1 character), or messages are spread on certain channels (RGB). Because the challenge title is Red Channel, the focus of the analysis is directed to the Red (R) channel.
title: Red Channel

content: 3. Verify with StegSolve To ensure that the data is indeed inserted in the red channel, one of the images is opened using StegSolve: java -jar stegsolve.jar img_000.png Then use the features: Data Extract check Red bit-plane 0 to 7 Extract By: Row Bit Order: MSB First The preview results show the hex byte 46 repeated.
title: Red Channel

content: 4. Convert Hex Values to ASCII The hex value 0x46 is the ASCII character: 0x46 → F When checked on the next image, the characters change sequentially: img_001.png → G * img_002.png → T * img_003.png → E * img_004.png → { So it can be concluded that: each image stores 1 character Characters are stored in Red channel
title: Red Channel

content: 5. Extraction Automation with Python To avoid having to open all images manually, extraction was performed using Python. Because the entire 0..7 bit-plane in the red channel is used, the character can be taken directly from the Red byte value at a particular pixel (for example (0,0) ). from PIL import Image import glob files = sorted(glob.glob("img_*.png")) flag = "" for f in files: im = Image.open(f).convert("RGB") r, _, _ = im.getpixel((0, 0)) flag += chr(r) print(flag)
title: Red Channel

content: TL;DR repeat is a crypto challenge from FGTE. —
title: repeat

content: Challenge Description The challenge provides a long ciphertext, with a hint: 13 -> 64 The question description also explains that the message is hidden in repeated encoding layers, so that after one layer is revealed, there is still another layer. From this hint it can be concluded that each layer uses a combination of: ROT13 Base64 which must be repeated continuously until the final plaintext appears.
title: repeat

content: Solution Steps
title: repeat

content: 1. Identify Transformation Patterns The ciphertext provided is still in the form of Base64 characters ( A–Z a–z 0–9 + / = ), but the final result cannot be read directly. Hint 13 -> 64 leads to process sequence: ROT13 ( 13 ) Base64 decode ( 64 ) Because the layers are repeated, this pipeline must be repeated several times until the result is no longer in Base64 form.
title: repeat

content: 2. Decrypt Using CyberChef (Recursive) The easiest way to do repeated decoding is to use CyberChef, because it provides a Jump feature to repeat the recipe. Recipe used: Label (as jump target) ROT13 3. From Base64 4. Jump (return to label to repeat) By configuration: ROT13: Amount = 13 - From Base64: default alphabet, non-alphabet chars removed Jump: Maximum jumps is increased so that the process can repeat several times
title: repeat

content: 3. Execute Decode Repeatedly After the recipe is run, the output changes layer by layer until it finally produces a string that matches the flag format.
title: repeat

content: Solution Steps
title: Reverse & Binary (Cryptography) — Writeup

content: 1. Reverse Ciphertext Because normal Base64 always puts = at the end, the first step is to reverse the string first. On CyberChef: Reverse (By Character) Once reversed, the format becomes valid Base64.

content: TL;DR scrambled is a misc challenge from FGTE. —
title: scrambled

content: Challenge Description The challenge provides an image that looks damaged/random (scrambled). The pattern in the image shows that the file is not corrupt, but is the result of the process of cutting the image into several tiles and then rearranging the tiles in a certain order (permutation). The objective of the challenge is to return the tile arrangement to its original position so that the image is readable again.
title: scrambled

content: Solution Steps
title: scrambled

content: 1. Identify the image size and grid pattern From the image file properties, we get the size: Width : 1280 Height : 854 The challenge uses a total of 16 tiles, so the most common grid is 4×4: 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 12 13 14 15 16 With this grid, tile sizes are calculated using integer division to be consistent with the scramble process: tw = w // 4 th = h // 4
title: scrambled

content: 2. Crop the image into 16 tiles The image is then cut into 16 parts based on the row reading order (left to right, top to bottom). Tiles are stored in memory so that there is no need to create output tile files one by one.
title: scrambled

content: 3. Determine permutation mapping After observing the results of the image arrangement, the following mapping was obtained: output_position → origin_tile 01 -> 13 02 -> 15 03 -> 09 04 -> 01 05 -> 14 06 -> 16 07 -> 10 08 -> 02 09 -> 03 10 -> 11 11 -> 05 12 -> 07 13 -> 04 14 -> 12 15 -> 06 16 -> 08 If visualized in grid form: 13 15 9 1 14 16 10 2 3 11 5 7 4 12 6 8 This means, for example, at the output position 01 we have to paste the tile number 13 , at the output position 02 paste the tile number 15 , and so on.
title: scrambled

content: 4. Image reconstruction based on mapping Once the tile is available, create a new canvas then paste the tile according to the mapping to the correct position, then save it as recovered.png .
title: scrambled

content: Script Solver (Python) from PIL import Image import sys pos_to_tile = { 1: 13, 2: 15, 3: 9, 4: 1, 5: 14, 6: 16, 7: 10, 8: 2, 9: 3, 10: 11, 11: 5, 12: 7, 13: 4, 14: 12, 15: 6, 16: 8 } img = Image.open(sys.argv[1]) w, h = img.size tw, th = w // 4, h // 4 tiles = {} idx = 1 for r in range(4): for c in range(4): tiles[idx] = img.crop((c * tw, r * th, (c + 1) * tw, (r + 1) * th)) idx += 1 out = Image.new("RGB", (tw * 4, th * 4)) for pos in range(1, 17): r, c = divmod(pos - 1, 4) out.paste(tiles[pos_to_tile[pos]], (c * tw, r * th)) out.save("recovered.png") print("[+] saved recovered.png")
title: scrambled

content: How to Run Install dependencies: pip install pillow Run solver: python3 solve.py scrambled.png The output will be saved as: recovered.png
title: scrambled

content: Results After the image is reconstructed, several candidate flags are visible in the final result. According to the challenge format, only one flag is valid and can be selected as the answer.

title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: Challenge Description The challenge provides a PGP encrypted message along with a keypair ( public_key.asc and private_key.asc ). The target is to decrypt message.asc to get the flag.
title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: Provided Files memo.txt - private_key.asc - public_key.asc - message.asc —
title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: Initial Analysis The message.asc file is a PGP (ASCII-armored) ciphertext. Because the private key is provided, the decryption process should be carried out directly, but the private key is protected with a passphrase. So the main step in this challenge is to find the passphrase of private_key.asc . Hint is in memo.txt : This motto often appears at the end of agents’ reports investigating unsolved mysteries. The motto that is very synonymous with the series The X-Files is: “Trust No One” In the context of passwords/passphrases, the most commonly used variations are: TrustNo1 - trustno1 - TrustNoOne For fast brute force, the wordlist can be narrowed down by taking relevant candidates from rockyou.txt .
title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: Exploitation / Solution
title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: 1. Create a Candidate Wordlist Instead of brute forcing the full rockyou.txt , a small wordlist of variations containing the keyword trustno is created. grep -i "trustno" /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt > wordlist.txt
title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: 2. Extract Hash Passphrase Private Key John the Ripper needed a hash extracted from the private key. The tool used is gpg2john . gpg2john private_key.asc > hash.txt
title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: 3. Crack Passphrase with John Once the hash is available, the passphrase can be searched using the narrowed wordlist. john --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt John’s output shows the correct passphrase: TrustNo1 (Agent 17)
title: Secret Agent’s Briefing

content: 4. Decrypt PGP Messages With the passphrase found, the message can be decrypted using gpg . gpg --batch --yes --pinentry-mode loopback \ --passphrase 'TrustNo1' \ --decrypt message.asc Output: ##Flags FGTE{REDACTED}

content: TL;DR Video QR is a misc challenge from FGTE. The QR output format looks like:
title: Video QR

content: Challenge Description The challenge provides a video file ( video.mp4 ) containing many QR codes. Each QR code does not contain a direct flag, but pieces of data that must be collected and reassembled. The QR output format looks like: IDX:000/67|<base64> IDX:001/67|<base64> ... This means that each QR carries 1 chunk of base64 data, with index IDX and total chunks /67 . ##Solution
title: Video QR

content: 1) Extract frames from video The first step is to break the video into a collection of images so that each QR code can be processed per frame. ffmpeg -i video.mp4 frames/frame_%05d.png
title: Video QR

content: 2) Decode QR of each frame After the frames are successfully extracted, each image is read using OpenCV and then decoded with pyzbar . To make the QR easier to read, the frame is upscaled and then converted to grayscale and threshold before processing. Scripts: import cv2 import glob from pyzbar.pyzbar import decode frames = sorted(glob.glob("frames/*.png")) seen = set() results = [] for f in frames: img = cv2.imread(f) if img is None: continue img = cv2.resize(img, None, fx=3, fy=3, interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC) gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY) _, th = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU) qr = decode(th) if not qr: continue data = qr[0].data.decode(errors="ignore") if data not in seen: seen.add(data) results.append(data) print(data) print("\nTOTAL UNIQUE:", len(results)) The output is saved: python3 decode_qr.py > output.txt
title: Video QR

content: 3) Rebuild base64 data from all chunks The contents of output.txt contain a QR snippet in the format: IDX:000/67|... The next step is to: parse all chunks mapping IDX -> chunk * reorder from 0..66 * combine base64 decode base64 into image file ( recovered.jpg ) Scripts: import re import base64 data = open("output.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore").read() parts = re.findall(r"IDX:(\d{1,3})/(\d+)\|([A-Za-z0-9+/=]+)", data) total_expected = int(parts[0][1]) mp = {} for idx, total, chunk in parts: mp[int(idx)] = chunk missing = [i for i in range(total_expected) if i not in mp] print("Expected:", total_expected) print("Got:", len(mp)) print("Missing:", missing) b64 = "".join(mp[i] for i in range(total_expected)) b64 += "=" * ((4 - len(b64) % 4) % 4) raw = base64.b64decode(b64) open("recovered.jpg", "wb").write(raw) print("Saved -> recovered.jpg") When executed, all chunks are successfully collected: Expected: 67 Got: 67 Missing: [] Saved -> recovered.jpg
title: Video QR

content: 4) Decode flags from last base64 When opening the file recovered.jpg there is a base64 encoded ciphertext which, if decoded, will produce a flag
title: Video QR

content: Check out the scoreboard! DO NOT ATTACK or scan the scoreboard; you don’t need to do that. TL;DR Scoreboard is a web reconnaissance challenge emphasizing the importance of examining raw HTTP response headers. The challenge instructions strictly prohibit aggressive fuzzing or vulnerability scanning. Requesting the server headers via curl -I reveals a custom HTTP header (x-flag) exposing the flag directly.
title: Scoreboard

content: Analysis The challenge description links to the CTF platform’s scoreboard endpoint: https://ctf.hackme.quest/scoreboard The author explicitly warns against port scanning, fuzzing, or attacking the application. This implies that the flag is not secured behind an exploit chain or authentication bypass, but is exposed through standard protocol metadata.

content: Inspecting HTTP Response Headers When troubleshooting or conducting passive reconnaissance on web applications, inspecting the HTTP headers sent by the server often discloses hidden server software versions, debug configurations, or embedded flags. We send a HEAD request using curl -I: curl -I "https://ctf.hackme.quest/scoreboard/?capture=the_flag" HTTP/2 200 server: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu) date: Wed, 11 Feb 2026 14:03:57 GMT content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 x-flag: FLAG{Header can hide some data aswell.} set-cookie: session_guard=623phcriikmfja7ag6o7k9l1mv; expires=Wed, 18-Feb-2026 14:03:57 GMT; Max-Age=604800; path=/; domain=ctf.hackme.quest; secure; HttpOnly expires: Thu, 19 Nov 1981 08:52:00 GMT cache-control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate pragma: no-cache The server response includes an anomalous custom response header: x-flag: FLAG{Header can hide some data aswell.}

content: Security Takeaway Custom and debug HTTP headers are often added during development for telemetry, routing, or staging verification. If left unmanaged, they can inadvertently disclose sensitive data, internal routing IDs, or software versions to untrusted clients. Always ensure production servers strip unneeded custom headers via web server reverse proxy rules.

content: Are overflows only possible on the stack? Explore how data behaves on the heap. TL;DR Heap 0 is an introductory heap exploitation challenge from picoCTF 2024. The program allocates two adjacent chunks on the heap: input_data and safe_var. Reading user input via an unbounded scanf("%s", input_data) allows an attacker to overflow past the allocated 5-byte chunk boundary, corrupting the subsequent safe_var chunk and fulfilling the win condition strcmp(safe_var, "bico") != 0.
title: Heap 0
Heap 0

content: Key Mechanisms Initialization (init): The binary calls malloc(5) for input_data and populates it with "pico". Immediately afterward, it calls malloc(5) for safe_var and populates it with "bico". Win Condition (check_win): If safe_var is modified such that strcmp(safe_var, "bico") != 0, the function reads and prints flag.txt. The Flaw (write_buffer): scanf("%s", input_data) reads an arbitrary-length string without width limits into a 5-byte heap chunk.
title: Heap 0

content: Memory Layout & Heap Analysis Running option 1 (Print Heap) displays the dynamic heap layout: Heap State: +-------------+----------------+ [*] Address -> Heap Data +-------------+----------------+ [*] 0x5eb3c90b4420 -> pico +-------------+----------------+ [*] 0x5eb3c90b4440 -> bico +-------------+----------------+
title: Heap 0

content: Offset Calculation input_data begins at 0x...420. safe_var begins at 0x...440. Distance: 0x440−0x420=0x20=32 bytes0x440 - 0x420 = 0x20 = 32 \text{ bytes}0x440−0x420=0x20=32 bytes Because of glibc malloc chunk alignment and metadata headers (chunk size and flags), the payload must travel 32 bytes to reach the data section of safe_var.
title: Heap 0

content: Exploitation To overwrite safe_var, we need to write at least 33 bytes: [ 32 bytes of padding ] + [ corrupting byte ]
title: Heap 0

content: Exploitation Steps Select option 2 (Write to buffer). Input a string exceeding 32 characters, such as 40 As (AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA). Select option 4 (Print Flag).

content: Flag picoCTF{b1tw^3se_0p3eR@tI0n_su33essFuL_d6f8047e}
title: Heap 0

content: Remediation Enforce Width Limits on Input: Replace unbounded scanf("%s", ...) with length-limited specifiers or safe functions: fgets(input_data, INPUT_DATA_SIZE, stdin); Bounds Checking: Always validate that the destination buffer has sufficient capacity before copying or reading data into it.

content: Kishor Balan tipped us off that the following code may require inspection. Can you find the secret pieces distributed across the web application? TL;DR Insp3ct0r is a classic introductory web challenge from picoCTF focusing on client-side code analysis. The application distributes the flag across three different web assets: HTML comments in the main index, CSS block comments in the stylesheet, and JavaScript comments in the client script. Inspecting all three files and concatenating their fragments reveals the full flag.
title: Insp3ct0r

content: Analysis The application landing page states that the website was built using standard web technologies: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) JS (JavaScript) The hint confirms that the flag has been split into 3 parts across these client-side resources.
title: Insp3ct0r

content: Step-by-Step Inspection
title: Insp3ct0r

content: Step 1: Inspecting the HTML Document We query the index page using curl : curl -s http://fickle-tempest.picoctf.net:54914/ Reviewing the HTML comments reveals part 1/3: <!-- Html is neat. Anyways have 1/3 of the flag: picoCTF{tru3_d3 --> The document also links to an external stylesheet ( mycss.css ) and script ( myjs.js ): <link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="mycss.css"> ... <script src="myjs.js"></script>

content: Security Takeaway Never leave sensitive operational data, API keys, internal endpoints, or developer comments in client-accessible assets. All HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are delivered in plaintext to the user’s browser and can be inspected effortlessly via browser developer tools or automated curl scripts.
